purpose: Authored source material for the aplayer phase expansion generator. Each entry is written once and composed into pages; the generator refuses to emit a page for any axis value that has no entry here. Contains no statistics, no third-party product claims, and no citations beyond the root URLs of organizations that unambiguously exist.

never miss twice.value: prevents one missed day from becoming identity-level drift
never miss twice.trigger: Use it the morning after a day you did not do the thing, while the miss is still a single event and not yet a story about who you are.
never miss twice.mechanism: A single miss costs you one day of output. The second consecutive miss is the one that rewrites the default, because it turns "I had a bad day" into "I am not doing this any more." The protocol treats day two as the only day with real leverage and spends nothing on day one.
moves: Write the miss down in one line with no explanation attached: date, what did not happen. Explanations are what turn a gap into a case.
Do not schedule a catch-up. Yesterday's block is gone and reclaiming it is what makes today fail too.
Name the smallest version of the same action that fits today, and put a time on it before you close the note.
Do that version today even if it is visibly smaller than usual. The point of today is the streak of participation, not the size of the output.

artifact.title: Miss-and-return ledger
rows: Day 0 (the miss)
Nothing. No analysis, no recovery plan, no promise about tomorrow.
One line: date and the action that did not happen.
Day 1 (the return)
Run the smallest valid version of the action, at a fixed time.

failure_modes.name: Doubling up to make the miss disappear
failure_modes.why: A doubled block is harder than a normal one, so the day after a miss becomes the hardest day of the week. That is the wrong incentive to attach to returning.
failure_modes.correction: Return at normal size or smaller. Never at larger.

failure_modes.name: Writing a post-mortem on day one
failure_modes.why: Analysis of a single miss produces a theory about yourself, and theories about yourself are much harder to miss twice against.
failure_modes.correction: Log the fact, skip the cause. Look for causes only after a third miss, where a pattern actually exists.

failure_modes.name: Restarting the count
failure_modes.why: Treating a miss as a reset to zero makes the count the thing you are protecting rather than the work.
failure_modes.correction: Track consecutive misses, not consecutive hits. The number you care about is never allowed above one.

never miss twice.not_this: It is not a streak tracker. A streak punishes the miss; this protocol is indifferent to the miss and interested only in the day after it.
never miss twice.evidence: At the end of the week, count how many times two misses landed back to back. That number, not the total days completed, tells you whether the protocol is working.
never miss twice.prompt: I missed yesterday. Do not analyze it. Give me the smallest version of the same action that fits today, and a time to start it.

minimum viable day.value: shrinks the day to one meaningful action when capacity is low
minimum viable day.trigger: Use it on a day where the honest read is that the normal plan is not going to happen, and the choice is between a smaller day and no day.
minimum viable day.mechanism: Most low-capacity days are lost to negotiating with a plan that was written for a different day. Naming a smaller day up front, in advance of the negotiation, removes the negotiation. The day still counts, and the system stays installed.
moves: Say the capacity out loud before you look at the list: what fraction of a normal day is actually available.
Pick exactly one output that would make today non-zero, and define its finished state in a sentence.
Delete or defer everything else in writing, so the deferral is a decision rather than a failure.
Stop when the one output is done, even if energy returns. Stopping on purpose is what makes the smaller day repeatable.

artifact.title: Minimum viable day card
rows: Capacity read
A fraction, stated before the list is opened.
Reading capacity after seeing the list produces a number that flatters the list.
The one output
One deliverable with a written finished state.
Two outputs is a normal day wearing a smaller name.
Explicit deferrals
The items you are not doing, listed by name.
Unlisted work does not go away; it stays as background pressure all day.
Stop condition
The moment the one output is finished.
Without a stop condition the small day expands and the next low day has no template.

failure_modes.name: Declaring a minimum day and then doing a normal one
failure_modes.why: It teaches you the minimum day was a lie, so the next time capacity drops you will not use it.
failure_modes.correction: Stop at the stop condition. If capacity returned, bank it as an early finish, not extra scope.

failure_modes.name: Choosing an output that is not actually meaningful
failure_modes.why: A trivial output makes the day technically non-zero and practically empty, which is worse than admitting a rest day.
failure_modes.correction: Pick the item you would be relieved to have done tomorrow morning.

failure_modes.name: Using it every day
failure_modes.why: A recovery protocol running as the default is just a smaller normal day, and capacity never gets rebuilt.
failure_modes.correction: Count the days you invoked it this month. Above roughly a third, the normal plan is the thing that needs resizing.

minimum viable day.not_this: It is not permission to do less indefinitely, and it is not a treatment for exhaustion or illness. It is a way to keep a system installed across a bad day.
minimum viable day.evidence: Record the one output and whether you stopped at the stop condition. Two fields, same two every time.
minimum viable day.prompt: Today is a low-capacity day. Ask me for my capacity as a fraction, then help me pick exactly one output and write its finished state.

no catch-up.value: closes missed work without turning yesterday into punishment
no catch-up.trigger: Use it when yesterday's undone list is about to be added on top of today's list.
no catch-up.mechanism: Undone work does not carry a deadline forward with it; it carries guilt forward. A carried list makes today structurally impossible, which produces another carried list. The rule forces an explicit disposition for every carried item so that today's list is a list someone could actually finish.
moves: Put yesterday's undone items in a separate place from today's plan. Never merge the two lists.
Give every carried item one of three dispositions: do today as a named block, reschedule to a named day, or drop.
Write the dropped items down as dropped. A deletion you can see is closure; a deletion you cannot see comes back as pressure.
Build today's plan only after the carried list is empty of undecided items.

Reschedule

Undecided

failure_modes.name: Merging the lists
failure_modes.why: Today plus yesterday is a list nobody finishes, so the day starts already failed and ends producing another carry-forward.
failure_modes.correction: Two lists, one pass, and today's list is written last.

failure_modes.name: Rescheduling to "this week"
failure_modes.why: An item without a specific day is an item that gets carried again, and the carry count is what generates the guilt.
failure_modes.correction: A named day or a drop. There is no third option.

failure_modes.name: Refusing to drop anything
failure_modes.why: If nothing can be dropped, the disposition pass is theatre and the list grows monotonically.
failure_modes.correction: Expect to drop items. A pass that drops nothing usually means the list is a wish record, not a plan.

no catch-up.not_this: It is not a productivity trick for getting more done. It usually results in less being done and more being finished.
no catch-up.evidence: Count carried items at the start of each pass. A working rule drives that number down over a week rather than flat or up.
no catch-up.prompt: Here is yesterday's undone list. Ask me to assign each item do-today, reschedule-to-a-named-day, or drop. Do not let me leave one undecided.

daily agenda engine.value: turns goals and constraints into a daily execution stack
daily agenda engine.trigger: Use it at the start of a day where you know roughly what matters but the list has no order and no fit to the hours available.
daily agenda engine.mechanism: Most daily plans fail on arithmetic rather than motivation: the list assumes more hours than the calendar contains. The engine takes fixed constraints first, subtracts them, and only then allocates the remainder, so the plan you leave with is one that fits the day you actually have.
moves: List fixed constraints first: meetings, travel, care obligations, anything already committed. These are not negotiable inputs.
Subtract them from the waking hours to get the real number of workable hours, then subtract a further margin for transition and overrun.
Fill the remaining hours with named outputs in priority order, stopping when the hours run out rather than when the list runs out.
Everything below the cut goes to the deferred list, in writing, before the day starts.

failure_modes.name: Planning against waking hours instead of workable hours
failure_modes.why: It produces a list that was impossible before the day began, and the failure gets attributed to discipline.
failure_modes.correction: Do the subtraction in writing every time. It takes two minutes and it is the whole method.

failure_modes.name: Ordering by urgency alone
failure_modes.why: Urgency ordering pushes the compounding work behind the loud work every single day.
failure_modes.correction: Order by consequence at the end of the month, then let urgency break ties.

failure_modes.name: No transition margin
failure_modes.why: Back-to-back allocation means the first overrun cascades and the afternoon is improvised.
failure_modes.correction: Reserve the margin explicitly and treat it as spent, not spare.

daily agenda engine.not_this: It is not a calendar tool and it does not schedule anything for you. It produces a plan that fits, which a calendar cannot check.
daily agenda engine.evidence: Compare planned outputs to completed outputs at the end of the day. A well-run engine converges those two numbers within a week or two.
daily agenda engine.prompt: Ask me for my fixed constraints today, subtract them and a transition margin from my waking hours, then help me fill only the remainder.

arbitration engine.value: chooses between competing priorities using leverage, urgency, energy, compounding, and downside
arbitration engine.trigger: Use it when two or more things genuinely deserve the same block and the tie is not breaking on its own.
arbitration engine.mechanism: Ties do not break by thinking harder, because the two options are close on the dimension you are thinking about. Scoring them on five named dimensions moves the comparison somewhere the difference is visible, and forces the trade to be stated rather than felt.
moves: Name the competing options explicitly, at most three. More than three is not arbitration, it is an unmade decision.
Score each on leverage, urgency, energy fit, compounding, and downside if skipped.
Say which dimension you are letting decide, before you look at the totals.
Write the losing option's next review date so it is parked rather than abandoned.

artifact.title: Five-dimension arbitration grid
headers: Why it is on the grid
rows: Leverage
Does finishing this make other work cheaper or unnecessary?
High-leverage work is systematically under-chosen because its payoff is indirect.
Urgency
Does a real external deadline exist, or an internal one?
Separating the two stops manufactured urgency from winning every tie.
Energy fit
Does this match the capacity actually available in this block?
A correct choice at the wrong energy level produces a stalled block.
Compounding
Does this get easier or more valuable if repeated?
Compounding work loses to urgent work every day unless it is scored.
Downside if skipped
What actually breaks if this waits a week?
Most items have a smaller downside than they feel like they have.

failure_modes.name: Scoring more than three options
failure_modes.why: Beyond three the grid becomes a research project and the block is spent on the grid.
failure_modes.correction: Cut to three by inspection first. The excluded items usually exclude themselves.

failure_modes.name: Letting urgency decide every time
failure_modes.why: Urgency is the loudest dimension, so unweighted use of the grid reproduces the pre-grid answer.
failure_modes.correction: Name the deciding dimension before totalling. If it is urgency twice in a row, check whether the deadlines are real.

failure_modes.name: Not parking the loser
failure_modes.why: An unparked option keeps re-entering the next decision, so the same arbitration is run repeatedly.
failure_modes.correction: Give the loser a review date at the moment it loses.

arbitration engine.not_this: It is not a prioritization framework for a whole backlog. It is a tie-breaker for a specific block, run in a few minutes.
arbitration engine.evidence: Record the option chosen and the deciding dimension. Reading a month of those two fields shows you what your system actually optimizes for.
arbitration engine.prompt: I have these competing options. Score each on leverage, urgency, energy fit, compounding, and downside if skipped, then ask me which dimension decides.

three-chat architecture.value: separates source-of-truth rules, daily runtime, and governance edits
three-chat architecture.trigger: Use it when one long assistant thread has become both the rulebook and the daily workspace, and the rules have started drifting.
three-chat architecture.mechanism: A single thread mixes three incompatible jobs: holding stable rules, running a disposable day, and deciding what the rules should be. The daily traffic pushes the rules out of context, so the rules quietly change without anyone deciding to change them. Splitting the three gives the rules a location that daily volume cannot displace.
moves: Create a rules chat that contains only the standing instructions. Never do daily work in it.
Create a runtime chat for today, seeded by pasting the rules block at the top. Discard it when the day ends.
Create a governance chat where proposed rule changes are argued and either accepted into the rules chat or rejected.
Change the rules only in the rules chat, and only from a decision made in the governance chat.

artifact.title: Chat responsibility split

Standing instructions, modes, boundaries, definitions.
Permanent. Edited deliberately and rarely.
Runtime
Today's plan, today's work, today's mess.
One day. Discarded without regret.
Governance

Ongoing. Produces decisions, not work.
Anything else

If a fourth chat appears, one of the three has lost its job.

failure_modes.name: Editing rules inside the runtime chat
failure_modes.why: A rule changed mid-day under pressure is a rule changed by the pressure, and it persists after the pressure is gone.
failure_modes.correction: Route the change through governance. Same-day rule changes are almost always mood.

failure_modes.name: Keeping the runtime chat for weeks
failure_modes.why: It accumulates contradictory context and starts producing answers based on a version of your situation that expired.
failure_modes.correction: Discard daily. The cost of re-seeding is one paste.

failure_modes.name: Rules that are too long to paste
failure_modes.why: If the rules block does not fit comfortably at the top of a runtime chat, it will stop being pasted, and the architecture collapses to one chat.
failure_modes.correction: Keep the rules short enough to re-seed in one action. Length is a design constraint, not an accident.

three-chat architecture.not_this: It is not a feature of any particular assistant product and does not depend on saved memory, projects, or custom instructions existing.
three-chat architecture.evidence: Track how often you re-seed the runtime chat from the rules chat. If the answer is rarely, the split has already failed.
three-chat architecture.prompt: Help me split my instructions into a rules block I can paste, and tell me which parts are runtime noise that should not be in it.

foreground priority.value: protects one project as the main execution target
foreground priority.trigger: Use it when several projects are all technically active and none of them is visibly moving.
foreground priority.mechanism: Parallel projects do not share time evenly; they share it in whatever proportion the day's noise dictates, which usually means none of them gets a block long enough to produce a result. Naming one foreground project does not stop the others; it decides in advance which one wins a contested block.
moves: Name one project as foreground for a stated period, measured in weeks rather than days.
Give every other active project an explicit background status with a maintenance floor: the minimum that keeps it from decaying.
When a block is contested, the foreground project takes it. This is the entire rule and its whole value is that it is decided in advance.
Review the foreground choice on a fixed date, not when a background project starts feeling urgent.

artifact.title: Foreground and background register
rows: Foreground
Every contested block, and the first block of the day.
No exemption from finishing; foreground status expires on a date.
Background, maintained
A stated minimum per week to stop decay.
Contested blocks, and any expansion of scope.
Background, paused
Nothing, and that is written down.
The pretence that it is progressing.
Unstatused
Not allowed. An unstatused project takes blocks by stealth.
Any claim on your time until it is given a status.

failure_modes.name: Two foreground projects
failure_modes.why: Two foregrounds means the rule never fires, because every contested block is still a fresh decision.
failure_modes.correction: One. If two feel mandatory, the honest read is that one of them is background with a large maintenance floor.

failure_modes.name: Rotating foreground weekly
failure_modes.why: A week is shorter than the feedback cycle of most real projects, so rotation guarantees nothing ever reaches evidence.
failure_modes.correction: Set the period long enough that the project can produce a result inside it.

failure_modes.name: Letting a background project become urgent and take over
failure_modes.why: Urgency-driven promotion is exactly the dynamic the rule exists to prevent.
failure_modes.correction: Handle the urgent item as a bounded interrupt with an end time. Do not re-designate foreground for it.

foreground priority.not_this: It is not a ban on other work. Background projects continue at their maintenance floor; they just stop winning contested blocks.
foreground priority.evidence: At the end of the foreground period, ask whether the project produced something that did not exist before. That is the only measure that matters here.
foreground priority.prompt: These are my active projects. Help me name exactly one as foreground for a stated period and give every other one a maintenance floor.

executive review mode.value: organizes known strategy without adding new theories
executive review mode.trigger: Use it when you already know most of what you need to know and the problem is that it is not organized into a decision.
executive review mode.mechanism: When a situation is unclear, the reflex is to gather more input, and more input makes an already-unstructured picture harder to act on. Review mode forbids new material and forces the existing material into a shape a decision can be made from.
moves: State the decision that is actually waiting, in one sentence ending in a verb.
List only what you already know that bears on it. New research is out of scope for the session.
Separate the list into facts, assumptions, and unknowns, and mark which unknowns would actually change the decision.
Make the decision, or name the single piece of information that would settle it and how you will get it.

Support the decision directly.
Assumption
You believe it and have not checked it.
Support the decision, but must be labeled.
Unknown, decision-changing
If it went the other way you would choose differently.
Justify delaying the decision. There are usually at most one or two.
Unknown, not decision-changing

failure_modes.name: Importing new information mid-session
failure_modes.why: It restarts the classification and the session ends with a bigger pile and no decision.
failure_modes.correction: Write new inputs on a separate sheet and finish the pass without them.

failure_modes.name: Treating every unknown as blocking
failure_modes.why: Most unknowns do not change the answer, and treating them as blocking is how a decision stays open for months.
failure_modes.correction: Apply the would-I-choose-differently test to each one explicitly.

failure_modes.name: Ending without a decision or a named settling fact
failure_modes.why: A review that produces neither is a session that converted anxiety into a document.
failure_modes.correction: Force one of the two outcomes before closing.

executive review mode.not_this: It is not strategy generation and it will not tell you something you did not already know. It converts what you know into a decision.
executive review mode.evidence: A completed pass ends with either a decision written in one sentence or one named fact with a method for getting it. Anything else is an incomplete pass.
executive review mode.prompt: Run executive review mode. Do not add new information. Ask me what I already know, sort it into fact, assumption, and decision-changing unknown.

high-pressure coaching mode.value: challenges avoidance when comfort language would keep the loop open
high-pressure coaching mode.trigger: Use it when you have described the same stuck situation more than twice and each description ends in reassurance rather than an action.
high-pressure coaching mode.mechanism: Supportive framing is correct for most situations and wrong for one: the loop where being understood is the reward, and the reward is available without doing the thing. Pressure mode removes the reassurance so the loop stops paying.
moves: Say the situation once, briefly, and ban the retelling.
Ask directly what you are avoiding and what it would cost to do it today.
Refuse abstractions. Every answer has to be a physical action with a time attached.
Set a check-in with a specific time, and treat the absence of evidence at that time as the answer.

New or genuinely complex problem

failure_modes.name: Using it as the default mode
failure_modes.why: Constant pressure stops carrying information, and you end up filtering it out the way you filter any constant signal.
failure_modes.correction: Reserve it for the specific repeated-loop condition.

failure_modes.name: Applying it to a capacity problem
failure_modes.why: Someone who cannot is not someone who will not, and pressure applied to the first is just an unpleasant way of getting nothing.
failure_modes.correction: Check capacity first. If capacity is the constraint, run recovery instead.

failure_modes.name: Confusing pressure with contempt
failure_modes.why: Contempt gives you a reason to stop using the system, which ends the loop by ending the system.
failure_modes.correction: Pressure is about the action and its cost. It is never about the person.

high-pressure coaching mode.not_this: It is not therapy, confrontation therapy, or a treatment for anything. It is a deliberately withheld reassurance in a narrow situation.
high-pressure coaching mode.evidence: Did a physical action with a time attached come out of the session, and did it happen? Two questions, asked at the check-in time.
high-pressure coaching mode.prompt: I have described this same stuck situation three times. Switch to pressure mode: no reassurance, ask what I am avoiding, and make me name a physical action with a time.

chief-of-staff logic.value: sequences priorities and converts ambiguity into next actions
chief-of-staff logic.trigger: Use it when the input is a pile of half-formed obligations rather than a list of tasks, and you cannot start because nothing is startable.
chief-of-staff logic.mechanism: A chief of staff's real function is not doing your work; it is converting things that are not yet actions into things that are, and putting them in an order. The layer does the same conversion in writing: every item leaves the pass either as a named physical action with an owner and a slot, or as an explicitly closed item.
moves: Dump every obligation in raw form, including the vague ones, without editing.
For each, ask what the physical next action is. If it cannot be named, the item is a decision, not a task, and gets routed to a decision block.
Assign each action an owner: you, someone else, or nobody, and be honest that nobody means it is not happening.
Sequence the actions that remain by what unblocks what, not by what is loudest.

"Open last quarter's invoices and list actual realized rates."
"Follow up with them"

failure_modes.name: Converting the easy items and leaving the vague ones
failure_modes.why: The vague items are the entire reason the pile is stuck; skipping them leaves the pile stuck with a shorter list on top of it.
failure_modes.correction: Do the vague ones first. They are the work.

failure_modes.name: Assigning actions to nobody
failure_modes.why: An unowned action reads as handled and is not, which is worse than an item you know is dropped.
failure_modes.correction: Owner is you, a named person, or dropped. There is no fourth value.

failure_modes.name: Sequencing by urgency
failure_modes.why: Urgency sequencing repeatedly runs blocked work before the thing that would unblock it.
failure_modes.correction: Sequence by dependency first, and use urgency only within a dependency tier.

chief-of-staff logic.not_this: It is not delegation and it does not create capacity. It converts ambiguity into actions, which frequently reveals that there are too many of them.
chief-of-staff logic.evidence: Count the items that left the pass without a physical next action. A working pass drives that to zero.
chief-of-staff logic.prompt: Here is a pile of half-formed obligations. For each, ask me the physical next action and the owner. If I cannot name one, route it to a decision block.

accountability mirror.value: compares stated commitments with observable completion evidence
accountability mirror.trigger: Use it when your sense of how the week went and what actually got finished have started to disagree.
accountability mirror.mechanism: Self-assessment drifts because it is scored on effort and intent, both of which are visible from the inside. The mirror scores only on artefacts, which are visible from the outside, and shows the gap between what was committed and what exists.
moves: Write the commitment before the period starts, in a form that can be checked without interpretation.
At the end of the period, list only what exists: files, sent messages, shipped changes, decisions recorded.
Put the two lists side by side and mark each commitment met, partially met, or not met.
Change one thing for the next period, and change the commitment rather than the effort.

failure_modes.name: Scoring effort
failure_modes.why: Effort is always available as an explanation, so any period can be scored as a success and the mirror stops reflecting anything.
failure_modes.correction: Score artefacts only. Effort goes in a separate note if you want it recorded.

failure_modes.name: Writing commitments that cannot be checked
failure_modes.why: An uncheckable commitment cannot be marked not met, so it never generates a correction.
failure_modes.correction: If two people could disagree about whether it was met, rewrite it.

failure_modes.name: Using the gap as evidence about yourself
failure_modes.why: That converts a measurement into a verdict and makes the next measurement something to avoid.
failure_modes.correction: The gap is information about the size of the commitment, and the fix is usually to make it smaller.

accountability mirror.not_this: It is not a performance review and it is not for anyone else to read. It is a measurement instrument, and instruments that shame you get switched off.
accountability mirror.evidence: The output is the met, partially met, and not met counts, and the one change you made to next period's commitments.
accountability mirror.prompt: Here is what I committed to this week. Ask me only for evidence that exists. Do not accept effort or intent, and mark each met, partial, or not met.

ambiguity stop.value: halts vague tasks until the physical action is named
ambiguity stop.trigger: Use it the moment you notice you have read the same list item three times without starting it.
ambiguity stop.mechanism: Re-reading without starting is a reliable signal that the item is not a task. It is a task-shaped container for an unmade decision or an unnamed action, and no amount of willpower converts one into the other. The rule stops the attempt and does the conversion instead.
moves: Stop trying to start. The re-reading is the diagnosis, not a discipline failure.
Ask what the first physical thing your hands would do. If there is no answer, the item is not a task.
If a decision is hidden inside it, extract the decision and make that the item.
Rewrite the item as the physical action, and leave the original phrasing next to it so the pattern is visible later.

failure_modes.name: Pushing through with willpower
failure_modes.why: It sometimes works and the cost is that you learn to spend your scarcest resource on a formatting problem.
failure_modes.correction: Treat the stall as a signal to convert, not to press harder.

failure_modes.name: Rewriting the item slightly and re-adding it
failure_modes.why: A reworded vague item is still vague, and the loop repeats with a new phrasing.
failure_modes.correction: The test is physical: can you describe what your hands do.

failure_modes.name: Splitting infinitely
failure_modes.why: Endless subdivision becomes its own avoidance, and the list grows while nothing starts.
failure_modes.correction: Split once, then start. Split again only if the first piece stalls.

ambiguity stop.not_this: It is not a planning method. It is an interrupt that fires on a specific observable symptom.
ambiguity stop.evidence: Note which items triggered the rule this week. Repeated triggers on the same kind of item tell you something about how you write tasks.
ambiguity stop.prompt: I have read this item three times without starting. Ask me what my hands physically do first, and if there is no answer, find the decision hidden in it.

first hour sequence.value: uses one physical start and one focused work block to break inertia
first hour sequence.trigger: Use it on mornings where the first hour reliably disappears into inputs and the real work starts after lunch or not at all.
first hour sequence.mechanism: The first hour sets the day's mode. An hour that begins with other people's requests establishes reactive mode, and reactive mode is hard to leave once the queue is visible. The sequence puts one physical action and one owned block before the inbox so the day starts in the other mode.
moves: Do one physical, non-screen action first. It exists to move you out of bed-state, not to be virtuous.
Read one pre-written card that names today's first output. Deciding at 7am with no context is how the hour is lost.
Work the first block on that output before opening any queue: mail, messages, feeds, tickets.
Open the queues only after the block ends, and treat what is in them as input to the rest of the day rather than a re-plan.

artifact.title: First hour ordering
rows: Physical start
One non-screen action, short.
Starting the day inside a feed.
The card
A sentence written the night before naming the first output.
Choosing at low context and defaulting to the easiest item.
First block
Work on that one output, queues closed.
Reactive mode being set before you have made anything.
Queues
Everything else, after the block.

failure_modes.name: A quick check of messages first
failure_modes.why: There is no such thing; the queue sets the mode on contact, and the block afterwards is spent thinking about the queue.
failure_modes.correction: Queues after the block. This is the load-bearing part of the sequence.

failure_modes.name: Building an elaborate morning routine around it
failure_modes.why: Additional habits make the sequence fragile, and a fragile sequence is abandoned in the first difficult week.
failure_modes.correction: Keep it to the four slots. Anything else is a separate project.

failure_modes.name: Not writing the card the night before
failure_modes.why: Writing it in the morning means deciding at the worst moment for deciding.
failure_modes.correction: One sentence, night before, physically visible.

first hour sequence.not_this: It is not a wellness routine and it makes no claim about sleep, exercise, or health. It is an ordering rule for the first sixty minutes.
first hour sequence.evidence: Record whether the first block happened before the queues opened. One binary field per day is enough to see the pattern.
first hour sequence.prompt: Help me write tonight's card: one sentence naming tomorrow's first output, short enough to read in five seconds.

recovery mode.value: protects continuity without pretending capacity is normal
recovery mode.trigger: Use it in a stretch of days where capacity is genuinely reduced and is not going to bounce back tomorrow.
recovery mode.mechanism: Reduced capacity handled by pretending produces a run of failed normal days, and a run of failed days ends the system. Declaring reduced capacity as a mode, with its own smaller standard, keeps the system installed through the stretch so there is something to return to.
moves: Declare the mode explicitly and give it an end date or a review date. An undeclared reduction is just a decline.
Set the reduced standard in writing: what a completed day looks like while the mode is on.
Suspend anything that only works at full capacity, by name, rather than letting it fail quietly.
Review on the date. Either exit the mode or extend it deliberately, and if you extend twice, get outside input.

artifact.title: Mode declaration record
rows: Reason
Stated plainly, without diagnosis.

Reduced standard
What counts as a complete day while the mode is on.
Without it the mode is just lower output with the old standard still judging it.
Suspended by name
The commitments that are off, listed.
Quiet failure of a commitment costs more than an explicit suspension.
Review date
A specific date.
A mode with no end date becomes the new normal without a decision.

failure_modes.name: Never declaring it
failure_modes.why: You run the normal standard against reduced capacity, fail daily, and attribute the failure to yourself.
failure_modes.correction: Declare it in writing. The declaration is most of the value.

failure_modes.name: No review date
failure_modes.why: The mode persists past the condition and the reduced standard becomes the standard.
failure_modes.correction: Set the date when you declare, not later.

failure_modes.name: Using it to avoid a decision
failure_modes.why: Sometimes what looks like reduced capacity is an unmade decision generating drag, and recovery mode makes it comfortable to keep not making it.
failure_modes.correction: Ask once whether there is a decision underneath. If there is, that is the work.

recovery mode.not_this: It is not treatment, and it is not advice about burnout, illness, or mental health. If the reason for the reduced capacity is health, that belongs with a qualified professional and this rule only governs the work commitments around it.
recovery mode.evidence: The record itself: reason, reduced standard, suspensions, review date, and what you decided on the review date.
recovery mode.prompt: I am running at reduced capacity for a while. Help me write a mode declaration: reduced standard, what I suspend by name, and a review date.

end-of-day check-in.value: closes the day with completed, partial, and missed evidence
end-of-day check-in.trigger: Use it at the end of any day you plan to draw a conclusion from, especially days that felt bad.
end-of-day check-in.mechanism: A day that is not closed gets remembered by its worst moment, and the plan for tomorrow gets written against that memory. Recording completed, partial, and missed separately gives tomorrow's plan an accurate input instead of an emotional one.
moves: List what is finished, meaning something exists that did not exist this morning.
List what is partial, and for each one write where it stopped so tomorrow starts at the edge rather than the beginning.
List what was missed, without explanations. The explanation is tomorrow's problem, not tonight's.
Write tomorrow's first output as a single sentence and stop.

artifact.title: Three-column close

An accurate read of actual throughput, which is usually higher than it felt.
Partial

Tomorrow's restart, which is the expensive part of resuming work.
Missed

The weekly pattern, where explanations would only obscure it.

failure_modes.name: Explaining the misses
failure_modes.why: Explanation at the end of a hard day produces a story about the week, and the story is what the next plan gets written against.
failure_modes.correction: Name them and stop. Look for patterns weekly, not nightly.

failure_modes.name: Percentages instead of stopping points
failure_modes.why: "Seventy per cent done" does not tell you where to put your hands tomorrow; the stopping point does.
failure_modes.correction: Record the exact place you stopped.

failure_modes.name: Turning it into a long journal
failure_modes.why: Length makes it skippable, and it is only useful if it happens on the bad days.
failure_modes.correction: Four fields, a few minutes. Optimize for surviving a bad day.

end-of-day check-in.not_this: It is not journaling or reflection practice. It is a data capture step that feeds tomorrow's first hour.
end-of-day check-in.evidence: The three columns themselves. A week of them is the input to any honest weekly review.
end-of-day check-in.prompt: Close my day. Ask me what is complete, what is partial and exactly where it stopped, and what was missed. Do not ask me why.

billionaire mindset track.value: filters opportunities through ownership, leverage, asymmetry, and downside containment
billionaire mindset track.trigger: Use it when an opportunity is in front of you and the question is whether it is worth entering at all.
billionaire mindset track.mechanism: Opportunities are usually evaluated on upside, which is the dimension the person presenting it has already optimized. Scoring ownership, leverage, asymmetry, and downside containment moves the evaluation to dimensions that determine whether the upside would ever reach you.
moves: Ask what you would own at the end, not what you would be paid during.
Ask whether the work is repeatable without you, or whether it stops the day you stop.
Ask whether the payoff distribution is asymmetric: is there a version where this is large.
Ask what the worst realistic outcome costs, and whether you can carry that cost without it ending other things.

artifact.title: Four-filter opportunity screen
rows: Ownership

Well-paid work that accumulates nothing.

A business that is a job with extra risk.
Asymmetry

Capped upside with uncapped time cost.
Downside containment

A bet whose bad case ends the other bets.

failure_modes.name: Using it to reject everything
failure_modes.why: Four filters applied strictly reject almost every real opportunity, and the framework becomes a sophisticated way to do nothing.
failure_modes.correction: It is a scoring pass, not a set of gates. Note where an opportunity is weak and decide with that visible.

failure_modes.name: Ignoring downside containment because the upside is large
failure_modes.why: An uncontained downside ends the sequence, and a sequence that ends does not compound.
failure_modes.correction: Score containment first. It is the only filter with a veto.

failure_modes.name: Treating it as investment advice
failure_modes.why: It is not. It is a structured way to ask four questions about your own time.
failure_modes.correction: Financial decisions with real money at stake belong with a qualified professional.

billionaire mindset track.not_this: It is not financial advice, investment guidance, or a claim about how anyone actually became wealthy. It is four questions applied in a fixed order.
billionaire mindset track.evidence: Record the four scores and the decision. Reviewing a year of screens shows which filter you habitually skip.
billionaire mindset track.prompt: Screen this opportunity on ownership, leverage, asymmetry, and downside containment. Ask about downside containment first.

continuity over intensity.value: prioritizes repeatable participation over heroic effort
continuity over intensity.trigger: Use it when planning a commitment you intend to keep for months, and the version you are about to commit to is the version you could do this week.
continuity over intensity.mechanism: Effort is elastic and schedules are not. A commitment sized to a good week fails in a normal one, and each failure costs more than the extra output of the good week bought. Sizing to the worst plausible week produces a commitment that survives, and surviving is what accumulates.
moves: Describe your worst plausible week honestly: illness, travel, a crisis at work.
Size the commitment so it is still doable in that week, not in this one.
Write the floor version explicitly, so that on a bad day there is something to do rather than a decision to make.
Let good weeks overflow, but never let the overflow raise the floor.

artifact.title: Sizing against the bad week

failure_modes.name: Raising the floor after a good stretch
failure_modes.why: It converts a sustainable commitment into one sized for conditions that will not persist, and the next bad week breaks it.
failure_modes.correction: Raise the floor only after several bad weeks cleared it easily.

failure_modes.name: Setting an embarrassingly small floor and abandoning it as pointless
failure_modes.why: The floor's value is that it is never missed, not that it is impressive.
failure_modes.correction: Judge the floor by whether it survived the bad week, not by how it reads.

failure_modes.name: Confusing the floor with the goal
failure_modes.why: The floor is the guarantee; the work still happens above it on most days.
failure_modes.correction: Keep both numbers visible: what you guarantee and what you are aiming at.

continuity over intensity.not_this: It is not an argument against hard work. Intensity is fine; it just cannot be the thing the system depends on.
continuity over intensity.evidence: Count the weeks the floor was met. A floor that has been missed more than rarely was set from a good week.
continuity over intensity.prompt: Ask me to describe my worst plausible week, then help me size this commitment so it still works in that week.

no mid-day renegotiation.value: keeps emotional volatility from rewriting the plan at 2 PM
no mid-day renegotiation.trigger: Use it on any day where the plan was made in the morning and the urge to rewrite it arrives in the afternoon.
no mid-day renegotiation.mechanism: The morning plan and the afternoon rewrite are made by the same person in different states. The afternoon state has more fatigue and less context about why the morning chose what it chose, so its rewrites systematically favor the easier item. Freezing the plan does not make the afternoon smarter; it stops the afternoon from deciding.
moves: Fix the plan in the morning and treat it as closed to changes from that point.
When the urge to rewrite arrives, write the proposed change down instead of making it.
Finish the current block anyway. The urge usually arrives at the hardest point of the block, not at a neutral moment.
Review the written proposals at the end of the day and let tomorrow's plan absorb the ones that still make sense.

failure_modes.name: Treating every mood as an external change
failure_modes.why: It makes the rule unenforceable, because there is always a justification available.
failure_modes.correction: External means something happened outside you that a third party could observe.

failure_modes.name: Discarding the proposal queue
failure_modes.why: Some afternoon judgments are correct and the queue is where you find out which.
failure_modes.correction: Read it nightly. It takes a minute and it stops the rule feeling arbitrary.

failure_modes.name: Applying it to a plan that was wrong from the start
failure_modes.why: Freezing a bad plan produces a wasted day and teaches you the rule is a trap.
failure_modes.correction: If the plan is wrong, stop and re-plan properly rather than drifting. That is a re-plan, not a renegotiation.

no mid-day renegotiation.not_this: It is not rigidity for its own sake. It moves plan changes to a moment when they can be judged, which is not the middle of a hard block.
no mid-day renegotiation.evidence: Keep the proposal queue. Over a few weeks it shows what fraction of afternoon rewrites you would have endorsed the next morning.
no mid-day renegotiation.prompt: It is mid-afternoon and I want to change the plan. Do not let me. Take the proposal down and hold it until my end-of-day review.

operator discipline.value: turns discipline into structure instead of self-criticism
operator discipline.trigger: Use it when the explanation for a repeated failure has become a statement about your character.
operator discipline.mechanism: Character explanations do not produce fixes, because there is no action that follows from them. Routing the same failure through structural questions produces the fix, and it turns out most repeated failures have a structural cause that was easier to see than to look for.
moves: State the failure as an event with a time and a place, not as a trait.
Ask the four structural questions: was it visible, was it scoped, was it scheduled, was it possible at that capacity.
Change the first structural answer that is no, and change only that one.
Observe for a stated period before concluding anything about yourself.

artifact.title: Structural cause checklist
rows: Was it visible?

Put it where your eyes already go.

Write the finished state before scheduling it.
Was it scheduled?
It was on a list but never in a block.
Give it a specific time, not a day.
Was it possible at that capacity?
The day did not have the hours or the energy.
Resize the commitment, not the effort.

failure_modes.name: Changing four things at once
failure_modes.why: You cannot tell which one worked, so the next failure has no information in it.
failure_modes.correction: One change, one observation period.

failure_modes.name: Skipping to the character explanation because it feels more honest
failure_modes.why: It feels honest because it is uncomfortable, but discomfort is not evidence and the explanation has no fix attached.
failure_modes.correction: Run the four questions first. Character is what is left after structure is exhausted, and it rarely comes to that.

failure_modes.name: Not setting an observation period
failure_modes.why: Without one, a single good day reads as fixed and a single bad day reads as proof of the trait.
failure_modes.correction: Name the period when you make the change.

operator discipline.not_this: It is not psychological assessment and it makes no claim about why anyone behaves as they do. It is four structural questions asked before a character explanation is allowed.
operator discipline.evidence: Record the failure, the failing structural answer, the one change, and the result after the observation period.
operator discipline.prompt: I keep failing at this and I am about to explain it with my character. Ask me the four structural questions first: visible, scoped, scheduled, possible.

strategic patience.value: prevents impulsive pivots before evidence is available
strategic patience.trigger: Use it when you are about to change direction and the current direction has not yet run long enough to produce evidence.
strategic patience.mechanism: Most pivots happen at the point of maximum discomfort, which is usually before the point of maximum information. The filter separates the two by asking what evidence would settle the question and whether it has arrived yet.
moves: Write down what evidence would tell you the current direction is wrong, in advance of looking for it.
Check whether that evidence has actually arrived, or whether what arrived is discomfort.
If the evidence has not arrived, name the date by which it would have, and hold until then.
If it has arrived, pivot deliberately and write down what you learned so the next attempt starts further along.

failure_modes.name: Writing the evidence test after the discomfort starts
failure_modes.why: A test written under discomfort is written to be passed by pivoting.
failure_modes.correction: Write it at the start, when you are indifferent.

failure_modes.name: Using the filter to justify never changing
failure_modes.why: Patience without a date is inertia, and inertia is as expensive as impulsiveness.
failure_modes.correction: Every hold needs a named end date.

failure_modes.name: Pivoting to something that has not been screened
failure_modes.why: An unscreened alternative is being chosen for its novelty, which is exactly what the filter exists to catch.
failure_modes.correction: Screen the alternative before it becomes the reason to leave.

strategic patience.not_this: It is not a rule against changing direction. It is a rule about when the decision has enough information in it.
strategic patience.evidence: The written evidence test, its date, and what you did when the date arrived.
strategic patience.prompt: I want to pivot. Ask me what evidence I wrote down in advance, whether it has arrived, and if it has not, help me set a hold date.

prompt pack installation.value: turns a normal LLM into a structured operating system
prompt pack installation.trigger: Use it when you have a set of instructions that work and you want them to apply reliably rather than when you remember to paste them.
prompt pack installation.mechanism: Instructions that live in your head are applied unevenly, and unevenly applied instructions produce inconsistent output that you then blame on the model. Installation makes the instruction set an artefact with a location, a version, and a re-seeding step, so applying it stops depending on memory.
moves: Write the instruction set as a single block that can be pasted in one action.
Give it a version marker so you can tell which version produced a given session.
Define the seeding step: what you paste, into what kind of chat, at what point.
Test it cold, in a fresh chat, before relying on it. Instructions that only work with prior context are not installed.

artifact.title: Installation checklist
rows: Single block
Pastes in one action.
Partial seeding, which behaves like different instructions each time.
Version marker
A date or number inside the block.
No way to attribute a behavior change to an edit.
Seeding rule
Stated: what, where, when.
The pack applies only when you happen to remember it.
Cold test
Works in a fresh chat with no prior context.
Depends on invisible context and breaks on a new device or account.

failure_modes.name: Relying on a product's memory or project feature
failure_modes.why: The behavior differs between products and changes between versions, so the pack stops being portable and starts being a configuration you cannot inspect.
failure_modes.correction: Keep the pack as pasteable text. Use product features as a convenience on top, never as the storage.

failure_modes.name: Editing the pack mid-session
failure_modes.why: The session's output can no longer be attributed to a version, and the edit was made under whatever pressure the session contained.
failure_modes.correction: Edit between sessions, bump the version.

failure_modes.name: A pack too long to paste
failure_modes.why: Length is the main reason packs stop being seeded.
failure_modes.correction: Cut it until seeding is frictionless. What you cut was probably not load-bearing.

prompt pack installation.not_this: It is not a claim about any assistant product's features, and it does not depend on a specific model, subscription tier, or interface staying the same.
prompt pack installation.evidence: Version marker, date installed, and whether the cold test passed.
prompt pack installation.prompt: Turn these instructions into a single pasteable block with a version marker, then help me test it cold in a fresh chat.

decision fatigue.value: reduces unnecessary choices before the day begins
decision fatigue.trigger: Use it when the decisions that feel hardest are small ones, which is the usual sign that the count is the problem rather than the difficulty.
decision fatigue.mechanism: Small decisions are cheap individually and expensive in aggregate, and the aggregate is invisible because no single one felt costly. Converting recurring decisions into standing defaults removes them from the day without anyone having to decide better.
moves: List the decisions you made yesterday that you also made the day before. Those are the recurring ones.
For each, write a default: what happens unless something specific overrides it.
Write the override condition too, so the default is a rule rather than a rut.
Re-decide only when the override condition fires, and review the defaults on a fixed schedule rather than continuously.

A relationship reason you can state in one sentence.
When to check messages

You are waiting on a specific reply you named in advance.

Only if declared before the list is opened.

failure_modes.name: Writing defaults without override conditions
failure_modes.why: A default with no override becomes a rule you break, and a rule you break undermines the others.
failure_modes.correction: Every default gets an override condition written at the same time.

failure_modes.name: Defaulting the decisions that actually matter
failure_modes.why: Consequential decisions are not the ones draining you, and defaulting them is how you sleepwalk into a bad outcome.
failure_modes.correction: Default only decisions that recur and whose downside is small.

failure_modes.name: Reviewing defaults constantly
failure_modes.why: Continuous review reintroduces the decision you removed.
failure_modes.correction: Fixed review schedule, and leave them alone in between.

decision fatigue.not_this: It is not a claim about willpower depletion or any specific mechanism in the brain. It is a way of reducing the number of choices in a day.
decision fatigue.evidence: Count the decisions converted to defaults, and how many times each override actually fired.
decision fatigue.prompt: Ask me which decisions I made both yesterday and the day before. For each, help me write a standing default and an override condition.

execution evidence.value: uses observable outcomes instead of intention as the source of truth
execution evidence.trigger: Use it when you need to know what is actually happening over weeks rather than what it feels like is happening.
execution evidence.mechanism: Memory of a period is reconstructed rather than recorded, and reconstruction is heavily weighted by the most recent and the most emotional days. A ledger written at the time is the only input to a review that is not itself a product of the review's mood.
moves: Record one line per working day: the output that exists, in a form someone else could verify.
Never record effort, intent, or how it felt. Those go elsewhere if you want them.
Review weekly by reading the lines, not by remembering the week.
Draw exactly one conclusion per review, and change one thing.

failure_modes.why: A backfilled week is a reconstruction, which is what the ledger exists to replace.
failure_modes.correction: Same day, or mark it as reconstructed so the review can discount it.

failure_modes.name: Recording effort when there was no output
failure_modes.why: It makes empty days look full and the ledger stops being able to show you anything.
failure_modes.correction: Write nothing. Days with nothing are the most informative entries in the ledger.

failure_modes.name: Reviewing daily
failure_modes.why: Daily review of a ledger produces mood-driven conclusions from a sample too small to contain a pattern.
failure_modes.correction: Weekly at minimum. Patterns need a week of days to be visible.

execution evidence.not_this: It is not a time tracker and it does not measure hours. It measures artefacts.
execution evidence.evidence: The ledger is the evidence. Its quality is measured by whether an entry could be checked by someone who was not there.
execution evidence.prompt: Take my ledger entry for today. Only accept something that exists and could be verified. Reject effort, intent, and progress language.

system drift recovery.value: restarts the system without shame analysis or reset theater
system drift recovery.trigger: Use it when a system you were running has quietly stopped and you are considering a full rebuild.
system drift recovery.mechanism: Drift is almost never total: most of the system is intact and one or two components stopped. A rebuild discards the intact parts along with the broken ones and costs a week, which is why the rebuild usually drifts too. Recovery finds the specific stopped component and restarts only that.
moves: List the components of the system as it was, without judging them.
Mark each one running, intermittent, or stopped, using evidence rather than memory.
Restart exactly one stopped component, the one the others depend on most.
Wait a week before restarting a second. Drift usually came from running more components than the week supports.

failure_modes.name: Full rebuild
failure_modes.why: It discards the working parts, costs a week of setup instead of a day of work, and the new system has the same load problem that caused the drift.
failure_modes.correction: Restart one component. The intact parts are an asset.

failure_modes.name: Restarting everything at once
failure_modes.why: The system drifted at that load once already; returning to full load reproduces the conditions.
failure_modes.correction: One component, one week, then reassess.

failure_modes.name: Analyzing why it drifted before restarting
failure_modes.why: The analysis becomes the project and the system stays stopped throughout it.
failure_modes.correction: Restart first. The cause is easier to see with something running.

system drift recovery.not_this: It is not a redesign step. Redesign is a separate activity and it should happen with the system running, not stopped.
system drift recovery.evidence: The component audit, the one component restarted, and whether it was still running a week later.
system drift recovery.prompt: My system drifted. Do not let me rebuild it. Ask me to list its components, mark each running, intermittent, or stopped, and restart exactly one.

capacity matching.value: fits work to current energy without abandoning the day
capacity matching.trigger: Use it when the block in front of you does not match the state you are actually in, and the choice looks like force it or lose it.
capacity matching.mechanism: Work has an energy profile and so does a block, and a mismatch produces a stalled hour that gets attributed to laziness. Keeping a categorized list means a mismatched block can be filled with work that fits rather than abandoned.
moves: Read your current state honestly and quickly: high, medium, or low. Do not negotiate with it.
Categorize your work the same way, in advance, so the matching does not require a decision when you are already low.
Take work from the matching category. A low block spent on low-category work is a productive block.
Note mismatches. Repeated mismatch at the same hour is a scheduling fact, not a discipline fact.

failure_modes.name: Categorizing in the moment
failure_modes.why: Deciding a category while low produces the category that justifies not working.
failure_modes.correction: Categorize in advance, when you are not choosing.

failure_modes.name: Only ever doing low work
failure_modes.why: High-category work never fits a low block, so it never happens and the important work is permanently deferred.
failure_modes.correction: Protect at least one high block a day and schedule it where your state is reliably high.

failure_modes.name: Treating low state as a moral failure
failure_modes.why: It adds a second problem to a capacity problem and does not change the capacity.
failure_modes.correction: Match and move. Investigate the pattern weekly, not in the block.

capacity matching.not_this: It is not an energy-management theory or a health claim. It is a categorization of your own work plus a matching step.
capacity matching.evidence: Record the state, the category you worked from, and whether the block produced something. Mismatches show up as a pattern within a couple of weeks.
capacity matching.prompt: Ask me my current state as high, medium, or low, then give me only work from my matching category. Do not suggest high work in a low block.

use ChatGPT to.label: using a general assistant chat
use ChatGPT to.surface: You are working inside an ordinary chat window with no saved setup. Whatever structure exists has to be typed into the message you are about to send.
use ChatGPT to.setup_cost: None. This is the mode you are already in, which is why it is the one people actually use.
use ChatGPT to.strength: Zero friction to start, and it works on any device, any account, any day.
use ChatGPT to.weakness: Nothing persists. The quality of the answer is set entirely by what you happened to type this time, so the same question gets a different answer on a different day.
use ChatGPT to.when_right: You need one answer now and you are not going to do this repeatedly.
use ChatGPT to.when_wrong: You have asked the same kind of question more than three times. At that point the retyping is the cost, and it is worth installing something.
table_rows: What you type
The full context every time: your situation, the constraint, and what a good answer looks like.
Omitting the constraint is why answers come back generic.
What the assistant knows
Only what is in this thread.
Do not assume it remembers a preference you stated last week in another chat.
What persists
Nothing.
Copy anything worth keeping out to a file before the thread scrolls.
When to leave this mode
After the third repeat of the same request.
Repetition is the signal to write the instruction down instead.
use ChatGPT to.first_line: Open a new chat and paste the whole situation, including the constraint you would normally leave out because it feels obvious.
use ChatGPT to.mistaken_for: A capability question. The capability is there; what is missing is anything that persists between sessions.
use ChatGPT to.wrong_metric: How good the last answer was. In this mode the next one is independent of it.
use ChatGPT to.first_week: Notice the third time you retype the same instruction. That is the signal to leave this mode.

use an LLM to.label: working with a language model as a generic capability
use an LLM to.surface: The question is about what a language model can do here at all, independent of which product you happen to have open.
use an LLM to.setup_cost: None, but you have to know which parts of the answer depend on the product and which do not.
use an LLM to.strength: Portable. Anything you build at this level survives changing products, subscriptions, and interface redesigns.
use an LLM to.weakness: It ignores the conveniences a specific product offers, so the workflow is sometimes more manual than it needs to be.
use an LLM to.when_right: You want the method to still work in a year, or you use more than one assistant.
use an LLM to.when_wrong: You have committed to one product and the convenience features would genuinely save you a step every day.
table_rows: Portable
Instructions written as text you paste.
Works everywhere, including a fresh account on a new machine.
Portable
Your own files holding the state.
The record survives the product.
Not portable
Saved memory, projects, custom instruction slots.
Convenient, but treat them as a cache of the portable version.
Not portable
Anything that depends on a specific button existing.
Interfaces change and the instruction becomes wrong without warning.
use an LLM to.first_line: Write the instruction as plain text you could paste anywhere, then decide separately whether to also store it in a product feature.
use an LLM to.mistaken_for: A product choice. At this level the product is the least important variable.
use an LLM to.wrong_metric: Which model is best this month, which changes and does not affect anything you would build here.
use an LLM to.first_week: Write your instructions as plain text and check they work in a product you do not normally use.

build a system to.label: designing a repeatable structure
build a system to.surface: The question is about design, not about today. You are deciding what will happen on a class of days, before any of them arrive.
build a system to.setup_cost: An hour or two once, plus the discipline of not redesigning it every week.
build a system to.strength: Removes the decision from the moment. On the day, there is nothing to work out.
build a system to.weakness: Systems designed in a good mood are sized for good days, and a system that only works on good days is worse than none.
build a system to.when_right: The situation recurs, and it recurs often enough that the design cost amortizes.
build a system to.when_wrong: This is a one-off, or you have already built three systems for it this year. Repeated building is usually avoidance of the running.
table_rows: Trigger
What starts it, stated as an observable event.
A system with no trigger runs when you remember, which is not a system.
Steps
The smallest sequence that produces the result.
Every step you add is a step that can fail on a bad day.
Evidence
What exists afterwards.
Without evidence you cannot tell whether it ran.
Failure branch
What happens on the day it does not run.
This is the part people skip, and it is the part that determines survival.
build a system to.first_line: Write the trigger first. Most systems that fail were never triggered by anything, so they ran only when the person felt like it.
build a system to.mistaken_for: A tooling exercise. Almost none of the design work is about which tool holds it.
build a system to.wrong_metric: How complete the design is. Systems designed to completeness are sized for good days.
build a system to.first_week: Write the trigger and the failure branch first, and leave the middle rough.

set up AI support to.label: configuring standing assistance
set up AI support to.surface: You are putting something in place that will be there tomorrow without being rebuilt: standing instructions, a stored template, a routine you can invoke by name.
set up AI support to.setup_cost: A short configuration session, plus a cold test in a fresh context.
set up AI support to.strength: It applies without you remembering to apply it, which is where most of the value is.
set up AI support to.weakness: Configuration is invisible once set, so a bad rule keeps operating silently until you go and read it again.
set up AI support to.when_right: The behavior you want is stable and you want it by default.
set up AI support to.when_wrong: You are still working out what you want. Configuring an unsettled preference makes it harder to change.
table_rows: Standing instruction
What should always be true of the responses.
Keep it short; long standing instructions get partially ignored.
Invocation
The phrase that starts the routine.
One phrase, memorable, used consistently.
Review date
When you will read the configuration again.
Configuration rots because nobody rereads it.
Cold test
Does it work in a fresh context with no history?
If not, it is depending on something invisible.
set up AI support to.first_line: Write the standing instruction, then open a completely fresh context and check it behaves the same way.
set up AI support to.mistaken_for: A one-time task. Configuration rots quietly because nobody rereads it.
set up AI support to.wrong_metric: How much you configured. Long standing instructions get partially ignored.
set up AI support to.first_week: Configure one thing, set a date to reread it, and test it in a fresh context.

create a daily operating system to.label: building a day-level operating loop
create a daily operating system to.surface: The unit is the day. The question is what happens at the open, what happens during, and what happens at the close, every day, in the same order.
create a daily operating system to.setup_cost: A design session plus roughly two weeks of running it before judging it.
create a daily operating system to.strength: Because it is the same every day, the parts that are wrong become visible fast.
create a daily operating system to.weakness: Day-level systems are the easiest to over-design, and every additional step multiplies across every day.
create a daily operating system to.when_right: Your days are structurally similar enough that one loop can cover them.
create a daily operating system to.when_wrong: Your days differ wildly in shape. Then the loop belongs at the week level with a small daily floor.
table_rows: Open
Read the card, name today's first output, check fixed constraints.
Under five minutes or it gets skipped on the days it matters most.
During
One protected block, then the rest of the day.
The protected block is the load-bearing part; everything else is negotiable.
Close
Complete, partial with stopping point, missed, tomorrow's first output.
Feeds tomorrow's open, which is what makes it a loop rather than a list.
Bad day branch
The floor version of the open and close, no protected block.
Without this, one bad day breaks the loop.
create a daily operating system to.first_line: Design the close before the open. The close is what makes the next open cheap, and it is the half that usually gets dropped.
create a daily operating system to.mistaken_for: Building a routine. A routine is a sequence; a loop is a sequence whose close feeds the next open.
create a daily operating system to.wrong_metric: How many steps it has. Every step multiplies across every day, including the bad ones.
create a daily operating system to.first_week: Run only the open and the close for a week and add nothing in between.

turn AI into a structure to.label: converting an open-ended tool into a bounded one
turn AI into a structure to.surface: The problem is not capability, it is that the tool will do anything, and anything is a bad default when you are trying to decide one thing.
turn AI into a structure to.setup_cost: The work of writing down constraints you have been holding implicitly.
turn AI into a structure to.strength: A bounded tool gives comparable answers across days, which is the precondition for noticing that something changed.
turn AI into a structure to.weakness: Constraints written too tightly produce answers that are technically compliant and useless.
turn AI into a structure to.when_right: Answers keep coming back plausible and unusable, which is the signature of an unbounded request.
turn AI into a structure to.when_wrong: You are exploring and do not yet know what good looks like. Constraints applied to exploration close it early.
table_rows: Scope constraint
What the answer must be about, and what it must not stray into.
Prevents the helpful tangent that eats the session.
Form constraint
The shape of the output: a table, three options, one sentence.
Form is most of what makes an answer usable.
Length constraint
A hard limit.
Unbounded length is how a decision request becomes an essay.
Refusal constraint
What it should say when the request cannot be answered well.
Without this you get a confident answer to an unanswerable question.
turn AI into a structure to.first_line: Write the form constraint first: say exactly what shape the answer must take before you describe the problem.
turn AI into a structure to.mistaken_for: Needing better prompts. Phrasing helps at the margin; constraints are what make an answer usable.
turn AI into a structure to.wrong_metric: How impressive the output reads. Plausible and unusable is the exact failure being fixed.
turn AI into a structure to.first_week: Add one form constraint to every request and change nothing else.

use A-player mode to.label: running the system's high-standard operating mode
use A-player mode to.surface: You are invoking a named mode with a fixed standard rather than asking an open question. The mode decides what counts as an acceptable answer.
use A-player mode to.setup_cost: Knowing the mode's rules well enough to notice when it has stopped following them.
use A-player mode to.strength: A named mode is checkable. You can tell when it has drifted, which you cannot with an unnamed style.
use A-player mode to.weakness: Modes drift silently as a thread lengthens, and drift is easy to miss because each step is small.
use A-player mode to.when_right: You want the same standard applied across sessions and you are willing to re-seed it.
use A-player mode to.when_wrong: The task genuinely needs a different standard. Forcing one mode onto everything is how modes stop meaning anything.
table_rows: Invocation
Name the mode explicitly at the start of the session.
An unnamed mode is a hope.
Standard
What the mode refuses to accept.
This is what distinguishes it from ordinary help.
Drift check
Re-read the mode rules mid-session.
Drift is the normal failure and it is silent.
Exit
Say when you are leaving the mode.
Otherwise the standard leaks into work it does not suit.
use A-player mode to.first_line: Name the mode in the first message and state the one thing it must refuse to accept from you today.
use A-player mode to.mistaken_for: A tone preference. A mode is a standard with a refusal attached, not a style.
use A-player mode to.wrong_metric: How the responses sound. Modes drift silently and the sound is the last thing to change.
use A-player mode to.first_week: Name the mode at the start of each session and re-read its rules halfway through.

use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.label: running the packaged system as installed
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.surface: The frameworks, modes, and boundaries are already written. The question is which one this situation calls for, not what to write.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.setup_cost: Installation once. After that the cost is choosing correctly.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.strength: The selection is the whole job, and selection is much cheaper than design.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.weakness: A packaged system invites running the framework you like rather than the one the situation needs.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.when_right: The situation matches a framework the system already contains.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.when_wrong: The situation is genuinely outside the system's scope, which includes anything clinical, legal, financial, or safety-related.
table_rows: Identify
What kind of situation is this: capacity, ambiguity, drift, or a tie?
Misidentification is the main source of a framework not working.
Select
The framework matched to that kind.
One framework per situation. Stacking them produces noise.
Run
Follow the moves as written, including the ones you would skip.
The skipped move is usually the one doing the work.
Boundary
Stop where the system's scope stops.
Educational and organizational only, with no exceptions for urgency.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.first_line: Say what kind of situation this is before naming a framework, because the identification is where the mistakes happen.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.mistaken_for: A question about what to write. The writing is done; the work is identifying which framework this is.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.wrong_metric: How many frameworks you used, which should usually be one.
use Billionaire High Performance Coach t.first_week: Before naming a framework, say what kind of situation this is: capacity, ambiguity, drift, or a tie.

install an execution system to.label: putting a system into daily operation
install an execution system to.surface: The design already exists. This is the part where it becomes something that actually runs, which is a different and harder problem than designing it.
install an execution system to.setup_cost: Low in effort, high in attention: installation fails on details like where the trigger lives.
install an execution system to.strength: Installation is where most of the value is realized, and it is the step most often skipped in favor of more design.
install an execution system to.weakness: An installed system is hard to see, so a broken component can run broken for weeks.
install an execution system to.when_right: You have a design that has survived contact with at least one real day.
install an execution system to.when_wrong: You are still redesigning. Installing an unsettled design means reinstalling repeatedly, which is how people conclude systems do not work for them.
table_rows: Location
Where the system physically lives.
If you have to remember where it is, it is not installed.
Trigger
What fires it, tied to something that already happens.
Attach it to an existing event rather than a new intention.
Minimum version
What running it looks like on the worst day.
Defined at install time, not discovered during a crisis.
Observation window
How long you run it before judging it.
Two weeks minimum. One bad week proves nothing.
install an execution system to.first_line: Decide where it physically lives and what already-happening event triggers it. Those two answers are the installation.
install an execution system to.mistaken_for: More design work. Installation and design are different jobs and the second is the one usually skipped.
install an execution system to.wrong_metric: How good the design is, which is not what determines whether it runs.
install an execution system to.first_week: Decide where it physically lives and which already-happening event triggers it.

run a daily protocol to.label: executing a fixed sequence on a schedule
run a daily protocol to.surface: Nothing is being designed or decided. There is a sequence, and the question is whether it ran today.
run a daily protocol to.setup_cost: None at run time. All the cost was paid when the protocol was written.
run a daily protocol to.strength: A protocol removes judgment from the moment, which is exactly what you want on the days judgment is expensive.
run a daily protocol to.weakness: Protocols that are too long stop running, and a protocol that runs at fifty per cent is often worse than a shorter one that runs completely.
run a daily protocol to.when_right: The sequence is settled and the value is in it happening every day rather than happening well.
run a daily protocol to.when_wrong: The situation is novel. Running a protocol against a new problem produces a completed protocol and an unsolved problem.
table_rows: Length
Short enough to complete on the worst day.
Length is the main predictor of whether a protocol survives.
Order
Fixed, and not re-decided in the moment.
Reordering is how a protocol becomes a decision again.
Completion mark
A visible record that it ran.
Without a mark you cannot tell a skipped day from a forgotten one.
Escape
