What to do when it genuinely cannot run.
A named escape prevents a missed day becoming an abandoned protocol.
run a daily protocol to.first_line: Time yourself running it once. If it takes longer than you would tolerate on a bad day, cut steps until it does not.
run a daily protocol to.mistaken_for: Discipline. A protocol exists so that discipline is not required at the moment of running it.
run a daily protocol to.wrong_metric: How thorough the protocol is. Length is the main predictor of whether it survives.
run a daily protocol to.first_week: Time yourself running it once and cut steps until it fits your worst day.

reduce decision fatigue.stall: The decisions that feel hardest are small ones — what to open first, whether to reply now, which of two near-identical tasks to start. That is the signature of volume rather than difficulty.
reduce decision fatigue.cause: Each of these decisions is individually cheap, so none of them registers as a cost, and the aggregate is therefore invisible while still being the thing that empties the afternoon.
reduce decision fatigue.first_move: List the decisions you made yesterday that you also made the day before, then write a standing default for each one with an explicit override condition.
reduce decision fatigue.wrong_move: Trying to make the small decisions faster. Speed on a decision that recurs daily saves seconds; removing it saves the decision.
reduce decision fatigue.measure: Count how many recurring decisions you converted to defaults, and how many times each override actually fired. Overrides that never fire mean the default was already right; overrides that fire constantly mean the default is wrong.
reduce decision fatigue.faq_q: How do I know a decision is worth turning into a default?
reduce decision fatigue.faq_a: Two tests: it recurred at least three times in the last week, and getting it wrong costs little. Decisions that recur but carry real consequence should stay decisions.
reduce decision fatigue.mistaken_for: Needing a better system. The system is usually fine and is being consulted forty times a day.
reduce decision fatigue.wrong_metric: Decisions made per day. Making more of them faster is the opposite of the fix.
reduce decision fatigue.first_week: Tally the decisions you made twice this week. Convert nothing yet; the tally is the diagnosis.

stop restarting goals.stall: There is a pattern of starting well, drifting after two or three weeks, and then restarting from the beginning with a new plan rather than resuming the old one.
stop restarting goals.cause: The restart is more attractive than the resume because a restart is clean and a resume requires admitting a gap. But restarting resets the accumulated position to zero every time, so the position never accumulates.
stop restarting goals.first_move: Take the last version and mark each of its components running, intermittent, or stopped, using evidence rather than memory. Then restart exactly one stopped component.
stop restarting goals.wrong_move: Designing a better system. The previous system was almost certainly good enough; it stopped running, which is a different problem and is not fixed by design.
stop restarting goals.measure: Count restarts per quarter. A working fix drives that number toward zero while the number of resumes goes up.
stop restarting goals.faq_q: What if the old system really was badly designed?
stop restarting goals.faq_a: Then it will fail again after you restart one component, and you will know which component, which is far more information than a fresh design gives you.
stop restarting goals.mistaken_for: A commitment problem. Each restart was committed to fully, which is why there have been several.
stop restarting goals.wrong_metric: How promising the new plan looks. Every restart looks promising on day one.
stop restarting goals.first_week: Do not write a new plan. Audit the last one and restart one stopped component.

choose the first task.stall: The list is visible, the hours are available, and the first twenty minutes go to deciding rather than working. Often the item chosen is the one that was easiest to start.
choose the first task.cause: Choosing at the start of a block means choosing at the moment you have the least context and the most inertia. The decision is being made in the worst possible conditions.
choose the first task.first_move: Write the first output the night before, as one sentence, somewhere you will physically see it in the morning. Do not decide in the morning.
choose the first task.wrong_move: Ranking the whole list. Ranking is a much larger task than choosing one item, and it is frequently how the block gets spent.
choose the first task.measure: Record whether the first block went to the item named the night before. That single binary field, over two weeks, tells you whether the problem is the choosing or the list.
choose the first task.faq_q: What if something urgent arrives overnight?
choose the first task.faq_a: Handle it as a bounded interrupt with a stated end time, then return to the named output. Replacing the named output should be a decision you make explicitly, not a drift.
choose the first task.mistaken_for: Not knowing your priorities. You usually do; you are deciding at the worst moment to decide.
choose the first task.wrong_metric: How quickly you start. Starting fast on the easiest item is the failure, not the fix.
choose the first task.first_week: Write tomorrow's first output tonight, in one sentence, somewhere you will physically see it.

recover after a missed day.stall: The day after a miss is spent either doing double or doing nothing, and both outcomes make the day after that harder.
recover after a missed day.cause: A miss carries no real deadline forward, only guilt, and guilt is answered either by over-correction or by avoidance. Neither is a plan.
recover after a missed day.first_move: Log the miss in one line with no explanation, do not schedule any catch-up, and run the normal-size version of the action today at a fixed time.
recover after a missed day.wrong_move: Doubling up. It makes the return day the hardest day of the week, which attaches a cost to returning.
recover after a missed day.measure: Count how often two misses land consecutively. That number is the only one that matters here; the total count of misses is not the problem.
recover after a missed day.faq_q: What if the missed work had a real deadline?
recover after a missed day.faq_a: Then it is not a missed habit, it is a late deliverable, and it gets re-planned as work with hours attached rather than run through a recovery rule.
recover after a missed day.mistaken_for: Losing discipline. One miss costs a day; the accounting for it costs the week.
recover after a missed day.wrong_metric: Longest streak, which makes the miss the event rather than the day after it.
recover after a missed day.first_week: Log any miss in one line, schedule no catch-up, and run normal size the next day.

protect one priority.stall: Several projects are technically active, all of them get some attention, and none of them has produced a visible result in weeks.
protect one priority.cause: Parallel projects share time in whatever proportion the day's noise dictates, which usually means no project gets a block long enough to reach a result.
protect one priority.first_move: Name one project foreground for a period measured in weeks, give every other active project a written maintenance floor, and let the foreground take every contested block.
protect one priority.wrong_move: Trying to give each project a fair share. Fairness at the project level produces failure at every project.
protect one priority.measure: At the end of the foreground period, ask whether something exists that did not before. That is the only measure; hours spent is not one.
protect one priority.faq_q: What happens to the background projects?
protect one priority.faq_a: They run at their maintenance floor, which is defined as the minimum that stops them decaying. That is a real commitment, just a small one, and it is written down so it does not silently become zero.
protect one priority.mistaken_for: A time problem. The blocks exist and keep going to whatever is loudest at the time.
protect one priority.wrong_metric: Hours on the project. A project can absorb hours without moving, and often does.
protect one priority.first_week: Name one foreground project and give it the first block of every day.

close the day with evidence.stall: Days end by simply stopping, and by the next morning the memory of the day has collapsed into how it felt rather than what happened.
close the day with evidence.cause: An unclosed day gets remembered by its worst moment, and tomorrow's plan gets written against that memory rather than against the actual output.
close the day with evidence.first_move: Write three columns at the end of the day: complete, partial with the exact stopping point, and missed with no explanation. Then one sentence naming tomorrow's first output.
close the day with evidence.wrong_move: Writing a reflective journal entry. Length makes it skippable, and it is only useful if it survives the bad days.
close the day with evidence.measure: Whether the close happened, as a binary, and whether tomorrow's first output was named. A close that happens only on good days provides no information.
close the day with evidence.faq_q: Why record the stopping point instead of a percentage?
close the day with evidence.faq_a: A percentage does not tell you where to put your hands tomorrow. The stopping point does, and restarting is the expensive part of resuming work.
close the day with evidence.mistaken_for: Needing to reflect more. Reflection produces feelings; the close produces tomorrow's input.
close the day with evidence.wrong_metric: How the day felt, which is set by its worst twenty minutes.
close the day with evidence.first_week: Run a three-column close in under three minutes, including on the days you do not want to.

avoid overplanning.stall: The plan gets refined repeatedly and the work does not start. Each refinement feels productive and produces no output.
avoid overplanning.cause: Planning is an activity with no failure state, which makes it a comfortable place to be when the work has one. More planning is therefore the path of least resistance and it is indistinguishable from progress from the inside.
avoid overplanning.first_move: Cap the planning: a fixed number of minutes, then the plan is closed and the first block starts regardless of how complete it feels.
avoid overplanning.wrong_move: Making the planning step better. A better planning process is a more comfortable place to stay.
avoid overplanning.measure: Time from opening the plan to starting the first block of actual work. Track it for a week; the number is usually surprising.
avoid overplanning.faq_q: How do I tell over-planning from genuinely needing to think?
avoid overplanning.faq_a: Genuine thinking changes the plan. If a planning session ends with substantially the same plan you started with, it was not thinking, and the next one will not be either.
avoid overplanning.mistaken_for: Being thorough. Thoroughness changes the plan; this leaves it substantially the same.
avoid overplanning.wrong_metric: Plan completeness, which has no ceiling and is therefore a comfortable place to stay.
avoid overplanning.first_week: Put a timer on planning and start the first block when it goes, whatever state the plan is in.

turn vague goals into actions.stall: The list contains items like sort out pricing or fix the process, and those items are read repeatedly and never started.
turn vague goals into actions.cause: They are not tasks. They are containers for unmade decisions, and no amount of willpower converts a decision into an action.
turn vague goals into actions.first_move: For each item, ask what your hands physically do first. If there is no answer, extract the decision hiding inside it and make the decision the item.
turn vague goals into actions.wrong_move: Rewording the item. A reworded vague item is still vague and the loop repeats with new phrasing.
turn vague goals into actions.measure: Count items that leave a planning pass without a physical next action. A working pass drives that to zero.
turn vague goals into actions.faq_q: What if the physical action is trivially small?
turn vague goals into actions.faq_a: That is the correct outcome. Open the file, list the three options, send the one-line message — these are what unstick the item, and their triviality is why they work.
turn vague goals into actions.mistaken_for: Procrastination. The item is not startable, which is a formatting problem rather than a willingness one.
turn vague goals into actions.wrong_metric: Items on the list. Vague items are cheap to add and never leave.
turn vague goals into actions.first_week: For every item you read twice without starting, write what your hands physically do first.

stay accountable without shame.stall: Accountability structures work for a while and then get quietly avoided, because checking in has become a place where you feel bad.
stay accountable without shame.cause: A structure that scores you rather than your commitments turns measurement into judgment, and judgment is something people route around.
stay accountable without shame.first_move: Score artefacts only: what exists that did not exist before. When something is not met, change the commitment rather than concluding something about yourself.
stay accountable without shame.wrong_move: Adding stakes or public consequences. Raising the cost of a miss raises the cost of looking, and not looking is the failure mode you are trying to prevent.
stay accountable without shame.measure: Whether you are still running the check-in after six weeks. Any accountability structure looks fine in week one.
stay accountable without shame.faq_q: Does removing the shame remove the accountability?
stay accountable without shame.faq_a: No. Accountability is the comparison between what you said and what exists. Shame is a reaction to the comparison, and it is the thing that makes people stop running it.
stay accountable without shame.mistaken_for: Needing higher stakes. Raising the cost of a miss raises the cost of looking, which is the actual failure.
stay accountable without shame.wrong_metric: How bad you feel about a miss, which correlates with nothing useful.
stay accountable without shame.first_week: Write three checkable commitments and score only artefacts. Add no stakes and no other person.

sequence a chaotic day.stall: The day contains real obligations at unpredictable times, and every plan built for it collapses before mid-morning.
sequence a chaotic day.cause: The plan was written against waking hours rather than workable hours, so it was arithmetically impossible before the day started.
sequence a chaotic day.first_move: List fixed constraints first, subtract them and a transition margin from the waking hours, and allocate outputs only against what remains.
sequence a chaotic day.wrong_move: Planning in more detail. A more detailed impossible plan is still impossible and takes longer to write.
sequence a chaotic day.measure: Compare planned outputs to completed outputs daily. Correct arithmetic converges those two within a week or two.
sequence a chaotic day.faq_q: What if the constraints themselves are unpredictable?
sequence a chaotic day.faq_a: Then budget for them as a block of unallocated time rather than pretending they will not happen. An unpredictable day still has a predictable amount of unpredictability in it.
sequence a chaotic day.mistaken_for: Needing a better calendar. The calendar accepts an impossible day without objection.
sequence a chaotic day.wrong_metric: How detailed the plan is. A detailed impossible plan is still impossible.
sequence a chaotic day.first_week: Write the workable-hours number at the top of the plan before writing the plan.

use AI without generic advice.stall: The answers come back reasonable, well organized, and useless — the kind of advice that would apply to anyone.
use AI without generic advice.cause: Generic input produces generic output. The constraint that makes your situation specific is usually the thing left out of the message, because it feels too obvious to state.
use AI without generic advice.first_move: Put the constraint in explicitly: the hours you actually have, the thing you cannot change, the option already ruled out and why.
use AI without generic advice.wrong_move: Asking for better or more specific advice without adding information. The response gets more confident, not more specific.
use AI without generic advice.measure: Whether the answer contains something that would be wrong for someone else in your rough situation. If it would suit anyone, it was generic.
use AI without generic advice.faq_q: What constraint is most often left out?
use AI without generic advice.faq_a: The one that feels too obvious to mention: the fixed obligation, the person whose agreement is required, the money that is not available. Obviousness to you is invisibility to anything you have not told.
use AI without generic advice.mistaken_for: A model quality problem. The same model gives specific answers when it is given the constraint.
use AI without generic advice.wrong_metric: Prompt length. Long prompts often carry less constraint than short ones that name a form.
use AI without generic advice.first_week: Add the constraint you normally leave out because it feels obvious, and compare the answers.

build consistency without streak pressur.stall: Streak tracking works until the streak breaks, and then the whole practice goes with it.
build consistency without streak pressur.cause: A streak makes the count the thing being protected. Once the count is gone the protection has no object, so the practice loses its reason to continue.
build consistency without streak pressur.first_move: Track consecutive misses instead of consecutive hits, and hold that number at or below one. A single miss costs nothing; the second consecutive one is the event.
build consistency without streak pressur.wrong_move: Restarting the streak from zero and trying harder. The restart re-establishes the same fragility.
build consistency without streak pressur.measure: Number of double misses per month. That is the number the practice actually depends on.
build consistency without streak pressur.faq_a: For a short defined push, yes, because there is an end date and the count expires with it. As an open-ended structure it makes the practice fragile at exactly the moment it needs to be robust.
build consistency without streak pressur.mistaken_for: Needing more willpower. What is missing is a floor small enough that bad days have an action.
build consistency without streak pressur.wrong_metric: Consecutive days, which cannot distinguish a robust practice from one that has not met a bad week.
build consistency without streak pressur.first_week: Define the floor and run only the floor, including on the days you could do more.

work when energy is low.stall: A block arrives, the state does not match the work, and the hour goes to rereading the same paragraph.
work when energy is low.cause: Work has an energy profile and so does a block. Mismatch produces a stalled hour, and the stall gets attributed to discipline rather than to the mismatch.
work when energy is low.first_move: Categorize your work as high, medium, or low in advance, then take work from the category that matches the state you are actually in.
work when energy is low.wrong_move: Forcing high-category work through a low block. It produces an unproductive hour and a conclusion about yourself, and neither is useful.
work when energy is low.measure: Record the state and the category worked. Repeated mismatch at the same time of day is a scheduling fact, not a character fact.
work when energy is low.faq_q: Doesn't this mean the hard work never happens?
work when energy is low.faq_a: Only if you never protect a high block. Schedule at least one where your state is reliably high, and let the matching rule govern the rest.
work when energy is low.mistaken_for: Laziness, which is a description rather than a diagnosis and comes with nothing to do.
work when energy is low.wrong_metric: Output on your best days, which sets a bar the low days will be judged against.
work when energy is low.first_week: Label each block high, medium, or low as you enter it, and note what it produced.

make a hard decision.stall: The decision has been open for weeks. Each time you return to it you rehearse the same considerations and stop in the same place.
make a hard decision.cause: Rehearsal is not analysis. The options are close on the dimension you keep thinking about, so thinking about that dimension harder cannot separate them.
make a hard decision.first_move: Score the options on leverage, urgency, energy fit, compounding, and downside if skipped, and name which dimension you are letting decide before you total anything.
make a hard decision.wrong_move: Gathering more information. Most of what you would gather does not change the answer, and gathering is a comfortable way to keep the decision open.
make a hard decision.measure: Whether the decision was made and written down with its deciding dimension. An unwritten decision reopens.
make a hard decision.faq_q: What if I genuinely lack information?
make a hard decision.faq_a: Apply the would-I-choose-differently test to each unknown. Usually one or two would change the answer and the rest would not, and only those one or two justify waiting.
make a hard decision.mistaken_for: Needing more information. Most of what you would gather does not change the answer.
make a hard decision.wrong_metric: How confident you feel. Confidence rises with rehearsal, which is not the same as analysis.
make a hard decision.first_week: Score the options on five named dimensions and say which one decides before you total.

separate urgency from pressure.stall: Everything feels urgent, and the things that get done are the loud ones rather than the consequential ones.
separate urgency from pressure.cause: Urgency and internal pressure produce the same sensation, so an internally generated deadline competes on equal terms with an external one and usually wins because it is closer.
separate urgency from pressure.first_move: For each item, ask what actually breaks if it waits a week, and who outside your head would notice. Real urgency has an external answer.
separate urgency from pressure.wrong_move: Working faster. Speed applied to a misordered list produces more of the wrong work.
separate urgency from pressure.measure: Track how many items scored as urgent had an external answer. A low proportion tells you the ordering is being set by pressure.
separate urgency from pressure.faq_q: Is internally generated urgency always wrong?
separate urgency from pressure.faq_a: No, but it should be labeled. Something can matter to you without having an external deadline, and labeling it that way stops it competing on a dimension it does not belong on.
separate urgency from pressure.mistaken_for: Poor prioritization. The ordering is fine; internally generated deadlines are competing as if they were external.
separate urgency from pressure.wrong_metric: How urgent something feels, which is exactly the signal being questioned.
separate urgency from pressure.first_week: For each urgent item, write who outside your head would notice if it waited a week.

finish a minimum viable day.stall: On low-capacity days the choice presents as the whole plan or nothing, and it usually resolves to nothing.
finish a minimum viable day.cause: The normal plan was written for a different day, and negotiating with it consumes the capacity that was available.
finish a minimum viable day.first_move: State the capacity before opening the list, name one output that would make today non-zero, write its finished state, and defer everything else in writing.
finish a minimum viable day.wrong_move: Doing a normal day at reduced quality. It produces a day that is neither finished nor rested, and no template for the next low day.
finish a minimum viable day.measure: Whether the one output was completed and whether you stopped at the stop condition. Two binary fields.
finish a minimum viable day.faq_q: What if energy returns after the one output is done?
finish a minimum viable day.faq_a: Bank it as an early finish. Expanding scope teaches you that the minimum day was not real, and the next time capacity drops you will not use it.
finish a minimum viable day.mistaken_for: Giving up on the day. A named smaller day is the opposite of abandoning it.
finish a minimum viable day.wrong_metric: Percentage of the plan completed, which makes a deliberately smaller day look like a failed normal one.
finish a minimum viable day.first_week: State capacity before opening the list, name one output, and stop when it is done.

keep context inside an LLM.stall: A long thread starts producing answers based on a version of your situation that expired weeks ago, and correcting it takes longer than starting over.
keep context inside an LLM.cause: One thread is holding stable rules, disposable daily work, and rule changes at the same time. Daily volume pushes the rules out and they drift without anyone deciding to change them.
keep context inside an LLM.first_move: Split into three: a rules chat that holds only standing instructions, a runtime chat discarded daily, and a governance chat where rule changes are argued.
keep context inside an LLM.wrong_move: Making the thread longer with more corrections. Corrections accumulate as contradictory context and the drift accelerates.
keep context inside an LLM.measure: How often you re-seed the runtime chat from the rules chat. If it is rare, the split has already collapsed.
keep context inside an LLM.faq_q: Doesn't the product's memory feature solve this?
keep context inside an LLM.faq_a: It helps with convenience and does not solve the drift, because memory features are not inspectable in the way a pasted rules block is. Keep the portable version as the source of truth and treat the feature as a cache.
keep context inside an LLM.mistaken_for: The assistant being unreliable. It is answering accurately from context that expired.
keep context inside an LLM.wrong_metric: Thread length, which feels like accumulated context and is usually accumulated contradiction.
keep context inside an LLM.first_week: Start each day in a fresh thread seeded from a written rules block.

restart without catch-up work.stall: Returning after a gap means facing an accumulated backlog, and the size of the backlog is what keeps the return from happening.
restart without catch-up work.cause: Undone work carries guilt forward rather than a deadline. Adding it to today makes today impossible, which produces another day of undone work.
restart without catch-up work.first_move: Put the backlog in a separate place, give every item one of three dispositions — do today, reschedule to a named day, or drop — and build today's plan only after the backlog holds nothing undecided.
restart without catch-up work.wrong_move: Merging the backlog into today's list. The merged list is one nobody finishes, so the day starts already failed.
restart without catch-up work.measure: Count carried items at the start of each pass. A working disposition rule drives that number down across a week.
restart without catch-up work.faq_q: Isn't dropping things just avoiding them?
restart without catch-up work.faq_a: Dropping is a decision with a record. Avoidance is an item that stays on the list and generates pressure without ever being worked. The second is far more expensive.
restart without catch-up work.mistaken_for: Needing to catch up. The backlog carries guilt rather than deadlines, and the two need different handling.
restart without catch-up work.wrong_metric: Size of the backlog, which grows while you look at it and tells you nothing about what to do.
restart without catch-up work.first_week: Give every carried item one of three dispositions and leave nothing undecided.

replace motivational planning.stall: Plans get made in a motivated state and executed in an ordinary one, and the ordinary state cannot carry them.
replace motivational planning.cause: A plan written while motivated is sized for the motivation. Motivation is not a resource you can schedule, so the plan is effectively sized for conditions that will not reliably recur.
replace motivational planning.first_move: Describe your worst plausible week and size the commitment so it still works in that week. Write the floor version explicitly so bad days have an action rather than a decision.
replace motivational planning.wrong_move: Trying to sustain the motivated state. It is not sustainable, and building on it means rebuilding after every dip.
replace motivational planning.measure: Count the weeks the floor was met. A floor missed more than rarely was set from a good week.
replace motivational planning.faq_a: It means guaranteeing lower and aiming the same. Good weeks still overflow above the floor; the difference is that the overflow never becomes the new baseline.
replace motivational planning.mistaken_for: Needing to want it more. The plan was sized for a state, and states are not schedulable.
replace motivational planning.wrong_metric: Your best week, which is the worst possible basis for a commitment.
replace motivational planning.first_week: Describe your worst plausible week and resize the commitment so it survives it.

build an operator rhythm.stall: Work happens in bursts followed by gaps, and the gaps get longer, so output is unpredictable and hard to plan around.
build an operator rhythm.cause: Burst working is sized to a state rather than to a schedule. Because the state is not repeatable on demand, neither is the output.
build an operator rhythm.first_move: Fix the shape of the day at three points — the open, one protected block, and the close — and hold those three constant while everything else varies.
build an operator rhythm.wrong_move: Scheduling the whole day. Full scheduling is fragile and breaks on the first real interruption, and once it breaks the rest of the day is improvised.
build an operator rhythm.measure: Whether the three fixed points happened, recorded daily as three binary fields. Rhythm is a frequency, so it can only be seen over weeks.
build an operator rhythm.faq_q: What if my days are genuinely different from each other?
build an operator rhythm.faq_a: Then the rhythm belongs at the week level with a small daily floor. The three fixed points still apply; they just take a few minutes rather than structuring the day.
build an operator rhythm.mistaken_for: Needing more structure. Full scheduling is fragile; three fixed points are not.
build an operator rhythm.wrong_metric: Adherence to the whole schedule, which breaks on the first real interruption.
build an operator rhythm.first_week: Hold the open, one protected block, and the close, and let everything else vary.

overwhelmed.signal: Every item on the list feels equally urgent, which is the reliable sign that none of them is being assessed.
overwhelmed.scarce: Attention, not time. The hours may exist; what is missing is the ability to hold one thing still long enough to work it.
overwhelmed.do_not: Do not re-plan. Re-planning under overwhelm produces a longer list and a stronger sense of how much there is.
overwhelmed.opening: Take one item off the list, out loud, and work it for twenty-five minutes without looking at the rest.
overwhelmed.after: The list is the same size and one item is smaller. That is the only reliable move from this state.
overwhelmed.mistaken_for: Having too much to do. Often the volume is survivable and the inability to hold one item still is not.
overwhelmed.wrong_metric: Length of the list. It stays the same length on the days you handle it well and the days you do not.
overwhelmed.first_week: Work one item for twenty-five minutes without opening the list. Repeat rather than re-planning.
overwhelmed.unit: One item, held still for twenty-five minutes without the rest of the list visible.
overwhelmed.looks_like_progress: Re-planning, which produces a longer list and a stronger sense of how much there is.

behind on commitments.signal: There is a set of things other people are waiting on, and the waiting is itself now part of the load.
behind on commitments.scarce: Credibility with the people waiting, which decays faster from silence than from lateness.
behind on commitments.do_not: Do not disappear until you can deliver. Silence costs more than a late delivery with a date attached.
behind on commitments.opening: Send the status messages before doing any of the work. One line each: where it is, when it lands.
behind on commitments.after: The load is unchanged and the pressure drops sharply, because most of it was the silence rather than the work.
behind on commitments.mistaken_for: A capacity problem. It is usually a communication problem first and a capacity problem second.
behind on commitments.wrong_metric: How far behind you are in days. The number grows while you look at it and does not tell you who to message.
behind on commitments.first_week: Send the status messages before doing any of the work, every day, until the outstanding list is visible to the people waiting.
behind on commitments.unit: One status message per waiting person, sent before any of the work.
behind on commitments.looks_like_progress: Working harder in silence, which is the thing making it worse.

stuck after a missed day.signal: Yesterday did not happen and today is being spent deciding what to do about yesterday.
stuck after a missed day.scarce: Nothing, actually. The capacity is there and it is being spent on the accounting.
stuck after a missed day.do_not: Do not schedule a catch-up and do not write a post-mortem on a single miss.
stuck after a missed day.opening: Log the miss in one line with no explanation, then run today's normal-size action at a fixed time.
stuck after a missed day.after: The miss stays a single event rather than becoming the first entry in a pattern.
stuck after a missed day.mistaken_for: Losing momentum. One missed day removes almost no momentum; the day spent accounting for it removes a lot.
stuck after a missed day.wrong_metric: Streak length. It makes the miss the event, when the day after is the only one with leverage in it.
stuck after a missed day.first_week: Log misses in one line with no explanation and run the normal-size action the next day. Nothing else.
stuck after a missed day.unit: Today, at normal size, run at a fixed time rather than when you feel ready.
stuck after a missed day.looks_like_progress: A catch-up plan, which makes the return day the hardest day of the week.

overplanning instead of executing.signal: The plan has been refined more than twice and no block of work has started.
overplanning instead of executing.scarce: Tolerance for starting something imperfect, which is what planning is substituting for.
overplanning instead of executing.do_not: Do not improve the planning process. A better planning process is a more comfortable place to stay.
overplanning instead of executing.opening: Close the plan on a timer, then start the first block with whatever the plan says at that moment.
overplanning instead of executing.after: The plan is worse than it could have been and something exists, which is the correct trade.
overplanning instead of executing.mistaken_for: Being thorough. Thoroughness changes the plan; this does not, which is how you can tell them apart.
overplanning instead of executing.wrong_metric: Plan quality. There is no ceiling on it, which is precisely why it is a comfortable place to stay.
overplanning instead of executing.first_week: Cap planning with a timer and start the first block when it goes, whatever state the plan is in.
overplanning instead of executing.unit: One block of actual work, started against an imperfect plan.
overplanning instead of executing.looks_like_progress: A better plan, which is a more comfortable place to stay.

tired of restarting.signal: This is at least the third version of the same system, and the previous versions are still recognizable in it.
tired of restarting.scarce: Belief that a system will hold, which each restart spends a little more of.
tired of restarting.do_not: Do not design version four. The previous versions were probably adequate and stopped running, which design does not fix.
tired of restarting.opening: Take the last version, mark each component running, intermittent, or stopped, and restart exactly one stopped component.
tired of restarting.after: One component runs and the rest of the intact system is still there, which a rebuild would have discarded.
tired of restarting.mistaken_for: Needing a system that suits you better. The previous ones usually suited you and stopped running.
tired of restarting.wrong_metric: How good the new plan looks. Every restart looks good on day one; that is the property that makes restarting attractive.
tired of restarting.first_week: Take the last version, audit its components, and restart one. Do not write anything new.
tired of restarting.unit: One stopped component of the previous version, restarted on its own and left alone for a week.
tired of restarting.looks_like_progress: Version four, which looks promising the way versions one to three did.

facing decision fatigue.signal: Small decisions are taking disproportionately long and the big ones are being deferred.
facing decision fatigue.scarce: Decision capacity for the day, most of which has gone to choices that recur and could have been defaults.
facing decision fatigue.do_not: Do not try to decide better. The problem is the count, not the quality.
facing decision fatigue.opening: Name the three decisions you have made today that you also made yesterday, and write a default for each.
facing decision fatigue.after: Tomorrow contains three fewer decisions, which is a permanent change rather than a better day.
facing decision fatigue.mistaken_for: Tiredness. It responds to removing choices rather than to rest, which is how you tell them apart.
facing decision fatigue.wrong_metric: Time of day. The afternoon slump gets blamed for what a morning of small decisions caused.
facing decision fatigue.first_week: Tally the decisions you make twice a day. Convert none of them yet.
facing decision fatigue.unit: One recurring decision, converted to a default with an override.
facing decision fatigue.looks_like_progress: Deciding faster, which is the opposite of removing the decision.

scattered across priorities.signal: Several projects are active, each has had some attention this week, and none has produced anything visible.
scattered across priorities.scarce: Contiguous blocks. Everything is getting minutes and nothing is getting an hour.
scattered across priorities.do_not: Do not try to give each project a fair share. Fairness at the project level produces failure at every project.
scattered across priorities.opening: Name one foreground project for a stated period and give the others a written maintenance floor.
scattered across priorities.after: One project moves visibly and the others are explicitly maintained rather than quietly stalled.
scattered across priorities.mistaken_for: Being busy. Busy produces output; scattered produces motion across several things and output in none.
scattered across priorities.wrong_metric: Projects touched. Touching four projects in a week is the symptom being measured as if it were progress.
scattered across priorities.first_week: Name one foreground project and give it the first block daily. Leave the others exactly as they are.
scattered across priorities.unit: One foreground project, for a period measured in weeks.
scattered across priorities.looks_like_progress: Touching every project this week, which is the symptom being measured as if it were output.

under launch pressure.signal: There is a date, the date is close, and the scope has not moved to match it.
under launch pressure.scarce: Days, which are fixed, against a scope that is not.
under launch pressure.do_not: Do not add hours. Hours borrowed against a launch are repaid immediately after it with interest.
under launch pressure.opening: Cut scope in writing to what fits the days that remain, and tell whoever needs to know before they find out.
under launch pressure.after: The launch is smaller and it happens, which is strictly better than the larger one that slips.
under launch pressure.mistaken_for: Needing to work harder. The scope has not been cut to fit the days, and effort does not close that gap.
under launch pressure.wrong_metric: Hours until launch. It counts down regardless of whether the scope moved, so it only raises pressure.
under launch pressure.first_week: Cut scope in writing to what the remaining days hold, and tell the people who need to know today.
under launch pressure.unit: The remaining days, with scope cut to fit them.
under launch pressure.looks_like_progress: Adding hours, which are borrowed against the week after the launch.

recovering from burnout.signal: Capacity is genuinely reduced, it has been for a while, and it is not going to bounce back tomorrow.
recovering from burnout.scarce: Capacity itself, which is the one input that cannot be reallocated from somewhere else.
recovering from burnout.do_not: Do not run the normal standard against reduced capacity. It produces a run of failed days and a conclusion about yourself.
recovering from burnout.opening: Declare a reduced-capacity mode in writing with a reduced standard, a list of suspended commitments, and a review date.
recovering from burnout.after: The system stays installed at a smaller size, so there is something to return to.
recovering from burnout.boundary: If exhaustion, low mood, or a change in how you are functioning persists, that belongs with a qualified professional. This is about the work commitments around it and nothing more.
recovering from burnout.mistaken_for: A discipline problem. Capacity and willingness are different, and pressure applied to the first produces nothing.
recovering from burnout.wrong_metric: Output compared to six months ago. Comparing a reduced-capacity period to a normal one produces a verdict, not information.
recovering from burnout.first_week: Declare the mode in writing with a reduced standard and a review date, and suspend by name what will not run.
recovering from burnout.unit: A declared mode with a reduced standard and a review date.
recovering from burnout.looks_like_progress: Returning to normal output, which is what produced the current state.

avoiding the hard task.signal: A specific item has been rescheduled repeatedly while everything around it gets done, often unusually promptly.
avoiding the hard task.scarce: Willingness to be bad at something in public, which is usually what the hard task actually requires.
avoiding the hard task.do_not: Do not reorganise around it. A well-organized avoidance is still avoidance and it now looks like progress.
avoiding the hard task.opening: Name what is actually at stake in the task, then define a version of it that takes twenty minutes and produces something visible.
avoiding the hard task.after: The task is started and smaller, and the thing at stake is written down rather than operating unnamed.
avoiding the hard task.mistaken_for: Procrastination in general. It is specific: one item is being avoided and the rest of the list is moving unusually well.
avoiding the hard task.wrong_metric: Total tasks done. It goes up during avoidance, which is what makes avoidance so easy to miss.
avoiding the hard task.first_week: Name what is at stake in the avoided task, then do a twenty-minute version that produces something visible.
avoiding the hard task.unit: Twenty minutes on the avoided item, producing something visible.
avoiding the hard task.looks_like_progress: Clearing everything around it, which rises during avoidance and hides it.

trying to build consistency.signal: The practice works for a stretch and then stops, and the stops are not caused by anything in particular.
trying to build consistency.scarce: A floor. There is a target and no defined minimum, so bad days have no version to run.
trying to build consistency.do_not: Do not raise the target. The target is not the problem; the absence of a floor is.
trying to build consistency.opening: Write the floor version: what running this looks like on the worst plausible day, small enough that it is never missed.
trying to build consistency.after: Bad days have an action instead of a decision, and the practice survives them.
trying to build consistency.mistaken_for: Needing more willpower. What is missing is a floor: a version small enough that bad days have an action rather than a decision.
trying to build consistency.wrong_metric: Days completed. It cannot distinguish a practice that survives a bad week from one that has not met one yet.
trying to build consistency.first_week: Define the floor and run only the floor, including on the days you could do more.
trying to build consistency.unit: The floor version, run on the worst day.
trying to build consistency.looks_like_progress: A higher target, which makes bad days impossible rather than small.

switching tools too often.signal: Setup has happened more recently than output, and there is a new tool in the last month.
switching tools too often.scarce: Accumulated state. Every switch discards the history that made the previous tool useful.
switching tools too often.do_not: Do not evaluate another tool. Evaluation is the activity that is substituting for the work.
switching tools too often.opening: Pick the tool you have the most history in, commit to it for a stated period, and write down what would have to be true to switch.
switching tools too often.after: A switch becomes a decision with criteria rather than a response to friction.
switching tools too often.mistaken_for: Being early to good tools. The tell is that setup has happened more recently than output.
switching tools too often.wrong_metric: How good the new tool is. It is usually better; that is not the question, and it never has been.
switching tools too often.first_week: Commit to the tool you have the most history in and write down what would have to be true to leave it.
switching tools too often.unit: One tool, committed to for a stated period with written switch criteria.
switching tools too often.looks_like_progress: Evaluating the next tool, which is the activity substituting for the work.

working without a chief of staff.signal: Half-formed obligations arrive faster than they can be converted into actions, and the pile is now the problem.
working without a chief of staff.scarce: Conversion capacity: the work of turning ambiguity into named actions, which nobody is doing.
working without a chief of staff.do_not: Do not try to do the pile. It contains items that are not doable because they are not yet tasks.
working without a chief of staff.opening: Run a conversion pass: for each item name the physical next action and the owner, and route anything without one to a decision block.
working without a chief of staff.after: The pile becomes a list of actions plus a short list of decisions, which is a much smaller problem.
working without a chief of staff.mistaken_for: Needing to hire. The conversion work can be systematized; the judgment and the relationships cannot.
working without a chief of staff.wrong_metric: How much is on your plate. It measures volume, not how much of the volume is not yet in a doable form.
working without a chief of staff.first_week: Run one conversion pass on ten items: physical next action and owner, or route to a decision block.
working without a chief of staff.unit: One conversion pass over ten items, each leaving with a physical next action or a routed decision.
working without a chief of staff.looks_like_progress: Reorganising the pile, which does not make unconverted items doable.

closing a chaotic week.signal: The week is ending, it does not feel like anything happened, and the memory of it is dominated by two bad days.
closing a chaotic week.scarce: An accurate record. What is left is a reconstruction weighted toward the worst moments.
closing a chaotic week.do_not: Do not plan next week from this feeling. A plan written against a bad reconstruction inherits the bad reconstruction.
closing a chaotic week.opening: List only what exists that did not exist on Monday, then read that list before writing anything about next week.
closing a chaotic week.after: Next week's plan is written against output rather than against mood, and the output is usually larger than the feeling suggested.
closing a chaotic week.mistaken_for: A bad week. Weeks that felt bad frequently produced more than weeks that felt fine, and only the record can tell you which.
closing a chaotic week.wrong_metric: How the week felt. It is reconstructed at the end and weighted by the worst two days in it.
closing a chaotic week.first_week: List what exists that did not exist on Monday, then read that list before planning anything.
closing a chaotic week.unit: The list of what exists that did not exist on Monday.
closing a chaotic week.looks_like_progress: Planning next week from how this one felt, which inherits the bad reconstruction.

starting at 2am.signal: The work is happening at hours that do not repeat, driven by whatever state made tonight possible.
starting at 2am.scarce: Repeatability. Output produced in an unrepeatable state cannot be planned around.
starting at 2am.do_not: Do not build a system around the good night. It is sized for a state you cannot schedule.
starting at 2am.opening: Capture what you produced, then set the smallest version of the same work at an hour that exists every day.
starting at 2am.after: The burst is banked and there is a repeatable version that does not depend on the burst recurring.
starting at 2am.mistaken_for: Being productive at night. The output is real and the state that produced it is not schedulable, which is the problem.
starting at 2am.wrong_metric: Output on the good night. Building a plan around it means the plan requires the night to recur.
starting at 2am.first_week: Bank what the burst produced and set the smallest version of the same work at an hour that exists every day.
starting at 2am.unit: The smallest version of the same work, at an hour that exists every day.
starting at 2am.looks_like_progress: Another good night, which is not schedulable and cannot be planned around.

preparing for a high-stakes day.signal: One day carries disproportionate consequence and the days before it are being consumed by anticipation.
preparing for a high-stakes day.scarce: Focus in the run-up, which anticipation takes without producing preparation.
preparing for a high-stakes day.do_not: Do not over-prepare. Past a point, preparation is anxiety management and it degrades the performance it is meant to support.
preparing for a high-stakes day.opening: List what would actually change the outcome, cap the preparation at that list, and schedule the rest of the run-up as ordinary work.
preparing for a high-stakes day.after: Preparation is bounded and the days before the event are not lost to it.
preparing for a high-stakes day.mistaken_for: Needing to prepare more. Past a point, preparation is anxiety management and it degrades what it is meant to support.
preparing for a high-stakes day.wrong_metric: Hours of preparation. It rises with anxiety rather than with readiness.
preparing for a high-stakes day.first_week: List what would actually change the outcome, cap preparation at that list, and treat the rest of the run-up as ordinary work.
preparing for a high-stakes day.unit: The short list of things that would actually change the outcome.
preparing for a high-stakes day.looks_like_progress: More preparation, which past a point is anxiety management.

juggling money pressure.signal: Financial constraint is present in every decision and is being carried rather than stated.
juggling money pressure.scarce: Room to be wrong. The constraint narrows the acceptable range of outcomes, which is a real change in the problem.
juggling money pressure.do_not: Do not plan as though the constraint is not there. An unstated constraint distorts every decision without appearing in any of them.
juggling money pressure.opening: Write the constraint down explicitly as an input, including the number and the date it bites.
juggling money pressure.after: Decisions are made with the constraint visible, which usually changes the ordering.
juggling money pressure.boundary: Decisions with real money at stake belong with a qualified professional. Nothing here is financial advice.
juggling money pressure.mistaken_for: A motivation problem. The constraint is real and it narrows the acceptable range of outcomes, which changes the problem.
juggling money pressure.wrong_metric: Revenue this month. It is the outcome you are trying to move and it tells you nothing about which action to take today.
juggling money pressure.first_week: Write the constraint as an input with a number and a date, and make this week's decisions with it visible.
juggling money pressure.unit: The constraint, written down with a number and a date.
juggling money pressure.looks_like_progress: Working more hours, which does not change the constraint and removes the room to think about it.

protecting a strategic project.signal: There is one project that matters more than the rest and it keeps losing blocks to things that are louder.
protecting a strategic project.scarce: Uninterrupted time, which is the one input the project needs and the one the day is worst at supplying.
protecting a strategic project.do_not: Do not rely on intention to protect it. Intention loses to urgency every time, in the moment, reliably.
protecting a strategic project.opening: Give it the first block of the day and a written rule that it takes every contested block.
protecting a strategic project.after: The protection is a rule decided in advance rather than a decision made under pressure.
protecting a strategic project.mistaken_for: Needing more time. The blocks exist and lose to louder work; more of them would lose the same way.
protecting a strategic project.wrong_metric: Hours logged against the project. A project can absorb hours without moving, and often does.
protecting a strategic project.first_week: Give it the first block of the day and a written rule that it takes every contested block.
protecting a strategic project.unit: The first block of the day, given to it by rule.
protecting a strategic project.looks_like_progress: Intending to protect it, which loses to urgency in the moment, reliably.

returning after drift.signal: The system stopped some time ago, the exact date is unclear, and returning feels like it requires an explanation.
returning after drift.scarce: A starting point. Everything is equally stopped so there is no obvious first move.
returning after drift.do_not: Do not analyze the drift before restarting. The analysis becomes the project and the system stays stopped.
returning after drift.opening: Restart one component today, chosen because the others depend on it, and leave everything else stopped for a week.
returning after drift.after: Something is running, and the cause of the drift is much easier to see with something running.
returning after drift.mistaken_for: Needing to start over. Most of the system is intact; a rebuild discards the intact parts along with the broken one.
returning after drift.wrong_metric: How long it has been. The number raises the cost of returning and gives you nothing to do.
returning after drift.first_week: Restart one component today and leave everything else stopped for the rest of the week.
returning after drift.unit: One component, restarted today, chosen because the rest of the system depends on it.
returning after drift.looks_like_progress: Understanding why it drifted, which becomes the project while the system stays stopped.

needing a lower-friction plan.signal: The plan is correct and it is not being followed, and the reason each time is a small piece of friction.
needing a lower-friction plan.scarce: Tolerance for setup steps. Each one is cheap and their sum is what stops the plan.
needing a lower-friction plan.do_not: Do not add discipline. Friction is a design property and discipline is an expensive way to pay for it daily.
needing a lower-friction plan.opening: Walk the plan and count the steps between deciding to start and actually starting. Remove the largest one.
needing a lower-friction plan.after: Starting costs less, which matters more than the plan being better.
needing a lower-friction plan.mistaken_for: Needing a simpler plan. The plan is usually fine; the steps between deciding to start and starting are not.
needing a lower-friction plan.wrong_metric: Plan complexity. A simple plan with four setup steps loses to a complex one with none.
needing a lower-friction plan.first_week: Count the steps between deciding to start and actually starting, and remove the largest one.
needing a lower-friction plan.unit: The steps between deciding to start and starting.
needing a lower-friction plan.looks_like_progress: Adding discipline, which is an expensive way to pay for a design problem every day.

decision fatigue.question: How do I stop spending the day's judgment on choices that repeat?
decision fatigue.move: Convert recurring low-consequence choices into standing defaults with written override conditions.
decision fatigue.evidence: The list of converted decisions, and how often each override fired.
decision fatigue.boundary_note: Fatigue that persists regardless of decision load is a health question, not a system question.
decision fatigue.mistaken_for: Being disorganised. The list is usually fine; it is the number of times a day you consult it that is not.
decision fatigue.wrong_metric: Hours worked. A day can be full and still end with nothing decided, and the hours will not show you that.
decision fatigue.first_week: Keep a tally of every decision you make twice. Do not change anything yet; a week of tallies is what tells you which three to convert.
decision fatigue.unit: A day, measured in decisions rather than hours.
decision fatigue.looks_like_progress: Deciding faster, which saves seconds on something that should not be decided at all.

missed-day recovery.question: What happens on the day after the thing did not happen?
missed-day recovery.move: Log the miss without explanation, refuse the catch-up, and run today's normal-size version at a fixed time.
missed-day recovery.evidence: Count of consecutive-miss pairs, not total misses.
missed-day recovery.boundary_note: A pattern of missed days driven by health belongs with a professional rather than a protocol.
missed-day recovery.mistaken_for: A motivation problem. It is a returning problem, and the two have opposite fixes.
missed-day recovery.wrong_metric: Longest streak. It says nothing about what happens after a break, which is the only thing that determines whether the practice lasts.
missed-day recovery.first_week: Miss one day deliberately and practice the return. Rehearsing the recovery while the stakes are zero is what makes it available when they are not.
missed-day recovery.unit: The single day after a miss. Nothing before it matters and nothing after it is decided yet.
missed-day recovery.looks_like_progress: A recovery plan, which is a second commitment made on the day you failed the first.

daily planning.question: How does a list become a plan that fits the day I actually have?
daily planning.move: Subtract fixed constraints and a transition margin from waking hours, then allocate only the remainder.
daily planning.evidence: Planned outputs against completed outputs, compared daily.
daily planning.mistaken_for: Needing a better tool. The tool is rarely the problem; the arithmetic between the list and the hours is.
daily planning.wrong_metric: Tasks completed. It rewards a day of small items over a day that moved one thing that mattered.
daily planning.first_week: Write the number of workable hours at the top of every plan before you write the plan. Nothing else changes this week.
daily planning.unit: One day, bounded by the hours actually available after commitments.
daily planning.looks_like_progress: A more detailed plan, which takes longer to write and is impossible in the same way.

accountability.question: How do I find out what I actually did rather than what I meant to do?
accountability.move: Write checkable commitments in advance and score only artefacts that exist afterwards.
accountability.evidence: Met, partial, and not-met counts, plus the one change made for the next period.
accountability.mistaken_for: Needing more discipline. It is almost always a measurement problem: what was committed was never written in a checkable form.
accountability.wrong_metric: How the week felt. Feeling is reconstructed at the end and weighted by the worst day in it.
accountability.first_week: Write three checkable commitments on Monday and read them on Friday. Do not add stakes, consequences, or another person yet.
accountability.unit: A week, because a day is too short to contain a pattern and a month is too long to correct.
accountability.looks_like_progress: Adding a consequence, which raises the cost of looking as much as the cost of missing.

priority selection.question: When two things both deserve this block, how does the tie break?
priority selection.move: Score on leverage, urgency, energy fit, compounding, and downside, and name the deciding dimension before totalling.
priority selection.evidence: The chosen option and the deciding dimension, recorded each time.
priority selection.mistaken_for: Not knowing what matters. Usually you know; what is missing is a rule for the moment two things both matter.
priority selection.wrong_metric: Number of priorities. Any list of priorities longer than one is a list of hopes with a strong word attached.
priority selection.first_week: Every time you pick between two things, write which one you picked and why. A week of those is a map of what your system actually optimizes for.
priority selection.unit: One contested block. Prioritizing a whole backlog is a different and much larger job.
priority selection.looks_like_progress: Ranking everything, which is usually how the contested block itself gets spent.

low-energy days.question: What work is the right work when the state does not match the plan?
low-energy days.move: Categorize work by energy profile in advance and take work from the matching category.
low-energy days.evidence: State, category worked, and whether the block produced something.
low-energy days.boundary_note: Persistently low energy is worth raising with a qualified professional rather than routing around.
low-energy days.mistaken_for: Laziness, which is a description rather than a diagnosis and comes with nothing to do about it.
low-energy days.wrong_metric: Output on the good days. It sets an expectation the bad days will be judged against and cannot meet.
low-energy days.first_week: Label each work block high, medium, or low as you enter it, and note whether it produced anything. Do not change your schedule yet.
low-energy days.unit: One block, matched to the state you are actually in when it starts.
low-energy days.looks_like_progress: Pushing through, which produces a stalled hour and a conclusion about your character.

execution review.question: What actually happened over the last period, as distinct from how it felt?
execution review.move: Read the written record rather than remembering, and draw exactly one conclusion per review.
execution review.evidence: The record itself, and the single change made after reading it.
execution review.mistaken_for: Needing to reflect more. Reflection produces feelings about the week; review produces a change to next week.
execution review.wrong_metric: How much you got through. Throughput hides whether the things you got through were the right ones.
execution review.first_week: Read last week from what exists rather than from memory, and write down exactly one change. Not three.
execution review.unit: A week of written record, read rather than remembered.
execution review.looks_like_progress: A longer review, which produces more conclusions and fewer changes.

founder overwhelm.question: Everything is mine and everything is urgent — where does the first cut go?
founder overwhelm.move: Separate items with an external consequence from items with an internal one, and order by the external answer.
founder overwhelm.evidence: The proportion of items scored urgent that had an external answer.
founder overwhelm.boundary_note: Sustained overwhelm that does not respond to reduced load is worth professional input.
founder overwhelm.mistaken_for: Needing to hire. Sometimes true, and usually the immediate problem is that nothing has been sorted into what only you can do.
founder overwhelm.wrong_metric: Inbox or backlog size. It grows regardless of how well the week went, so it cannot tell you anything about the week.
founder overwhelm.first_week: Split the list once into work only you can do and work that has an owner or could have one. Do not act on the split yet, just make it.
founder overwhelm.unit: The list, split once into what only you can do and what has an owner.
founder overwhelm.looks_like_progress: Reorganising the list, which changes its shape and not its size.

context retention.question: How does the assistant stop working from a version of my situation that expired?
context retention.move: Separate stable rules from disposable daily runtime, and re-seed the runtime from the rules rather than extending a thread.
context retention.evidence: How often the runtime context is re-seeded from the rules block.
context retention.mistaken_for: The assistant being unreliable. The context it is working from expired, which is a setup problem rather than a capability one.
context retention.wrong_metric: Thread length. A long thread feels like accumulated context and is usually accumulated contradiction.
context retention.first_week: Start each day in a fresh thread seeded from a written rules block, and note when re-seeding costs you anything real.
context retention.unit: One session, seeded from a written block and discarded at the end of it.
context retention.looks_like_progress: A longer thread, which accumulates contradiction and feels like accumulated context.

prompt structure.question: Why do the answers come back plausible and unusable?
prompt structure.move: State the form the answer must take and the constraint that makes the situation specific, before describing the problem.
prompt structure.evidence: Whether the answer contains something that would be wrong for someone else in a similar situation.
prompt structure.mistaken_for: Needing better prompts. Phrasing helps at the margin; the missing constraint is what makes the answer generic.
prompt structure.wrong_metric: Length of the prompt. Long prompts often carry less usable constraint than short ones with a form specified.
prompt structure.first_week: Before sending, add one line stating the shape the answer must take. Change nothing else and compare the results.
prompt structure.unit: One request, with its form and its constraint stated before the problem.
prompt structure.looks_like_progress: A longer prompt, which usually carries less usable constraint than a short one.

behavioral follow-through.question: Why does the thing that was decided not get done?
behavioral follow-through.move: Ask whether it was visible, scoped, scheduled, and possible at that capacity, and change the first answer that is no.
behavioral follow-through.evidence: The failing structural answer, the one change, and the result after a stated observation window.
behavioral follow-through.mistaken_for: A character flaw. Four structural questions account for most of it, and character explanations come with nothing to change.
behavioral follow-through.wrong_metric: Completion rate. It averages over items that were impossible and items that were merely unscheduled, which need different fixes.
behavioral follow-through.first_week: For each thing that did not happen, write which of visible, scoped, scheduled, or possible was false. Just the tally.
behavioral follow-through.unit: One failure, examined against four structural questions before any conclusion about character.
behavioral follow-through.looks_like_progress: Trying harder, which is the response that produced the current situation.

weekly planning.question: What is the week for, given that most of it is already committed?
weekly planning.move: Fix the week's commitments first, then place at most three outputs against the remainder.
weekly planning.evidence: Outputs placed against outputs completed, read at the end of the week.
weekly planning.mistaken_for: Needing to plan more. Most weeks are over-planned and under-subtracted.
weekly planning.wrong_metric: Number of items placed. It measures ambition at the start of the week, which is the least informative moment.
weekly planning.first_week: Place at most three outputs for the week and leave the rest unplaced. Read what happened on Friday before changing the number.
weekly planning.unit: A week whose commitments are fixed first and whose outputs are placed against the remainder.
weekly planning.looks_like_progress: More items placed, which measures ambition at the least informative moment of the week.

restarting after failure.question: How do I resume without rebuilding from the beginning?
restarting after failure.move: Audit components as running, intermittent, or stopped, and restart exactly one stopped component.
restarting after failure.evidence: Which component was restarted and whether it was still running a week later.
restarting after failure.mistaken_for: Needing a better system. The old one usually worked and stopped, which design does not address.
restarting after failure.wrong_metric: How different the new plan is from the old one. Novelty is not evidence of improvement, and it is expensive.
restarting after failure.first_week: Audit the old system's components against evidence and restart exactly one. Leave the rest stopped for the full week.
restarting after failure.unit: One component of the old system, restarted on its own.
restarting after failure.looks_like_progress: A new system, which discards the working parts and costs a week of setup.

chief-of-staff support.question: Who turns this pile of half-formed obligations into actions?
chief-of-staff support.move: Run a conversion pass giving every item a physical next action and an owner, or routing it to a decision block.
chief-of-staff support.evidence: Count of items leaving the pass without a physical next action.
chief-of-staff support.mistaken_for: Needing to be more organized. The pile is not disorganised, it is unconverted: it contains things that are not yet tasks.
chief-of-staff support.wrong_metric: Items processed. Moving a vague item between lists counts as processing it and changes nothing.
chief-of-staff support.first_week: Take ten items and name the physical next action for each. Count how many had no answer; that count is the actual problem.
chief-of-staff support.unit: One pass over the pile, converting each item into an action or a decision.
chief-of-staff support.looks_like_progress: Moving items between lists, which counts as processing and changes nothing.

cost and access.question: What does this actually require, and what happens if I cannot pay for the convenient version?
cost and access.move: Separate what the method needs from what a particular product offers, and keep the method in a form that works without the product.
cost and access.evidence: Whether the workflow survives a cold test with no paid features available.
cost and access.mistaken_for: A pricing question. It is usually a portability question: what happens to your setup if the paid feature goes away.
cost and access.wrong_metric: Monthly cost. It ignores the switching cost you take on when the workflow depends on one product's conveniences.
cost and access.first_week: Run your normal workflow once with every convenience feature switched off, and write down what actually broke.
cost and access.unit: The workflow, run once with every paid convenience switched off.
cost and access.looks_like_progress: Finding a cheaper product, which changes the price and not the dependency.

private journaling boundaries.question: What should and should not go into a tool I do not control?
private journaling boundaries.move: Decide the categories in advance — work state and commitments in, personal health and third-party information out — and write the line down.
private journaling boundaries.evidence: The written category list, and whether it was applied without renegotiation in the moment.
private journaling boundaries.boundary_note: Anything you would not want stored or processed by a third party should not be typed into one, and that judgment is yours to make in advance rather than while writing.
private journaling boundaries.mistaken_for: A trust question about one product. It is a categories question, and it should be settled before any product is chosen.
private journaling boundaries.wrong_metric: Whether a provider says data is private. What matters is what you decided to put in before you read the policy.
private journaling boundaries.first_week: Write the two lists — what goes in, what stays out — before your next session, and keep them somewhere you will see.
private journaling boundaries.unit: Two written lists, decided before the session rather than during it.
private journaling boundaries.looks_like_progress: Reading a privacy policy, which is useful and does not decide what you put in.

task sequencing.question: What order should these go in, given that some unblock others?
task sequencing.move: Sequence by dependency first and use urgency only to break ties within a dependency tier.
task sequencing.evidence: Whether blocked work was attempted before its unblocking item.
task sequencing.mistaken_for: A prioritization problem. Priority says which matters; sequence says which has to happen before which, and they disagree often.
task sequencing.wrong_metric: How many items are in progress. Concurrent work looks like momentum and usually means several blocked things.
task sequencing.first_week: Draw the dependencies once for the current set of work. Most lists have two or three real chains and a lot of independent items.
task sequencing.unit: A dependency chain, drawn once for the current set of work.
task sequencing.looks_like_progress: Starting more things, which looks like momentum and usually means several are blocked.

motivation dependency.question: What happens on the days the motivation is not there?
motivation dependency.move: Size the commitment against the worst plausible week and write the floor version explicitly.
motivation dependency.evidence: Count of weeks the floor was met.
motivation dependency.mistaken_for: Needing more discipline, which is the same request as needing more motivation with a sterner word attached.
motivation dependency.wrong_metric: Best week ever. Sizing a commitment against your best week guarantees it fails in an ordinary one.
motivation dependency.first_week: Write the floor version of your main commitment and run only that, even on the days you could do more.
motivation dependency.unit: Your worst plausible week, which is what the commitment has to survive.
motivation dependency.looks_like_progress: A stronger commitment, which raises the size of the thing that will fail.

system drift.question: How did this stop running without anyone deciding to stop it?
system drift.move: Audit each component against evidence rather than memory, and restart one at a time with a week between.
system drift.evidence: The component audit and the restart record.
system drift.mistaken_for: Losing interest. Most drift is load: the system was running more components than the week supports.
system drift.wrong_metric: How long since it last ran. It tells you it stopped and nothing about which part stopped first.
system drift.first_week: List the components and mark each running, intermittent, or stopped from evidence. Restart nothing in week one.
system drift.unit: Each component, marked running, intermittent, or stopped from evidence.
system drift.looks_like_progress: Rebuilding, which is the most expensive response to the cheapest kind of failure.

strategic focus.question: How does the important work stop losing to the loud work?
strategic focus.move: Name one foreground project for a period measured in weeks and give it every contested block by rule.
strategic focus.evidence: Whether the foreground project produced something that did not exist at the start of the period.
strategic focus.mistaken_for: A time-management problem. The hours usually exist; what is missing is a rule for who wins a contested block.
strategic focus.wrong_metric: Time spent on the strategic project. Time is not the output, and a project can absorb hours without moving.
strategic focus.first_week: Name one project foreground and give it the first block of every day. Change nothing else about the week.
strategic focus.unit: One contested block, and the rule that decides it in advance.
strategic focus.looks_like_progress: Time logged against the project, which a stalled project accumulates as readily as a moving one.

founder.context: Every unowned item defaults to you, and the list of unowned items grows faster than the list of things you can hand off.
founder.constraint: There is no one above you setting the priority, so the ordering is a job you do in addition to the work.
founder.hardest: Distinguishing the work that only you can do from the work that arrived first.
founder.scene: a founder with three unowned items and one investor update due
founder.mistaken_for: Needing to delegate. Often true eventually, and today the problem is that nothing has been sorted by who can do it.
founder.wrong_metric: Hours worked, which for a founder is always high and therefore always uninformative.
founder.first_week: Split this week's work once into what only you can do and what has an owner. Act on nothing yet.
founder.week_shape: No two weeks have the same shape, and the parts that repeat are the ones you scheduled rather than the ones that matter.
founder.protect: The first block of the day, before anyone else's requests have arrived and set the agenda.
founder.advice_that_fails: "Delegate more." It assumes a sorted list and an existing team, and the sorting is the work that has not happened.
founder.vignette: It is 09:40. The investor update is due Friday, two hires are waiting on a decision that only they can make, and a customer email arrived that will take an hour to answer properly. Nothing on that list has an owner other than them.

solo operator.context: You are the whole operation: delivery, admin, sales, and the switching between them.
solo operator.constraint: Context switching is your largest hidden cost and it does not appear on any list.
solo operator.hardest: Protecting a block long enough to finish delivery work before an admin item interrupts it.
solo operator.scene: a solo operator whose delivery block keeps getting eaten by invoicing
solo operator.mistaken_for: Needing better tools. Switching costs are what a solo operation can least afford.
solo operator.wrong_metric: Number of things handled, which rises with switching and falls with focus.
